name: Fenghuangopterus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation of Liaoning, China.
• Described by Lü Junchang and colleagues in 2010.
• Represented by a single, beautifully preserved skeleton.
• Named after the Fenghuang, a mythological Chinese bird.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation of Liaoning, China, named after the mythical Phoenix (Fenghuang) of Chinese tradition.","Characterized by a unique dental configuration where the anterior teeth are sharply recurved and separated by wide, regular diastemata.","Possessed a stiffened, elongate tail that comprised over 60% of its total body length, providing immense directional stability during aerial banking.","Foraged in lush, temperate conifer forests interspersed with freshwater lakes, capturing flying aquatic insects and small lake fish."]

name: Liopleurodon
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation, England or France.
• Described by Henri Émile Sauvage in 1873.
• Name means smooth-sided tooth, referring to its tooth enamel.
• Gained fame through its exaggerated depiction in Walking with Dinosaurs.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered throughout the Middle-to-Late Jurassic Oxford Clay of England and France, measuring roughly 5 to 7 meters in total length.","Possessed four massive, hydrofoil-shaped flippers that generated propulsion via subaqueous flight, utilizing all four flippers for explosive acceleration.","Its 1.2-meter skull was armed with colossal, smooth-enameled, deeply socketed teeth up to 10 centimeters long, capable of crushing armor and bone.","Hydrodynamic and sensory modeling indicates that Liopleurodon had directional stereoscopic olfaction, pinpointing prey scents carried across marine currents."]

name: Plesiosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by Mary Anning in Lyme Regis, England, in 1823.
• Described by William Conybeare in 1824.
• The first complete plesiosaur skeleton ever found.
• Its name means near lizard.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in 1823 by legendary fossil hunter Mary Anning in the Early Jurassic Blue Lias cliffs of Lyme Regis, Dorset, England.","Its iconic body plan featured a tiny head, an immensely long neck constructed of roughly 40 cervical vertebrae, and four broad paddle-like flippers.","The famous paleontologist William Buckland famously described it as resembling 'a turtle with a serpent threaded through its body'.","Its jaws were packed with sharp, slender, intermeshing needle-like teeth, perfectly tailored for impaling belemnites, ammonites, and small pelagic fish."]

name: Ichthyosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by Mary Anning in Lyme Regis, England, in the early 19th century.
• Described by Charles König in 1818.
• The first fully recognized genus of the ichthyosaur group.
• Its name translates to fish lizard.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered by Mary Anning and formally described by Charles König in 1818, serving as the name-bearing type genus of Ichthyosauria.","Possessed a streamlined, porpoise-like body with a crescent-shaped tail fluke, propelled by powerful lateral beats of its hypocercal caudal fin.","Its huge orbital sockets housed massive bony sclerotic rings, which prevented eyeball deformation and assisted deep-water visual hunting.","Exceptional fossil slabs preserve complete silhouettes of its dorsal fin and skin outlines, proving that ichthyosaurs possessed a fleshy dorsal fin devoid of bone."]

name: Ophthalmosaurus

discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation of England.
• Described by Harry Govier Seeley in 1874.
• Hundreds of specimens have been discovered worldwide.
• The name means eye lizard.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated in immense numbers from the Oxford Clay of Peterborough, England, measuring roughly 5 meters in length.","Possessed the largest eyes relative to body size of any known vertebrate, with eye sockets measuring up to 22 centimeters in diameter.","Equipped with immense sclerotic rings composed of 15 interlocking plates, enabling it to hunt bioluminescent squid in the pitch-black oceanic mesopelagic zone.","Adult specimens were virtually toothless, relying on rapid buccal expansion to suction feed on belemnites and soft cephalopods in deep waters."]

name: Cryptoclidus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation, England.
• Described by Harry Govier Seeley in 1892.
• Name means hidden collarbone, referring to its small clavicles.
• Known from numerous excellent skeletons.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Oxford Clay of England, measuring roughly 3 to 4 meters in total body length.","Possessed an elongated neck of 32 vertebrae terminating in a delicate skull armed with roughly 100 slender, needle-like interlocking teeth.","Its teeth were angled outward, creating an efficient underwater sieve designed to trap small fish, decapod crustaceans, and squid.","Possessed broad, wing-like flippers with flattened propodials (humeri and femora) that maximized thrust during four-winged underwater flapping."]

name: Rhomaleosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Alum Shale Formation of Yorkshire, England.
• Described by Harry Govier Seeley in 1874.
• The most famous specimen is named the Barrow Kipper.
• Name means strong lizard.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in 1848 in the Alum Shale of Whitby, Yorkshire, England, measuring approximately 7 meters in length.","A massive, large-headed rhomaleosaurid pliosaur that served as the undisputed apex macropredator of the Early Jurassic European epicontinental seas.","High-resolution CT scanning revealed paired directional olfactory chambers in its snout, allowing it to sample underwater scents flowing through internal nostrils.","Its neck was moderately long and reinforced by interlocking cervical ribs, allowing it to violently shake and dismember large marine reptiles."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Rhomaleosaurus cramptoni description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhomaleosaurus"}]

name: Macroplata
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Blue Lias Formation in Warwickshire, England.
• Described by William Elgin Swinton in 1930.
• The holotype includes a nearly complete skeleton.
• Its name means big plate, referring to its large shoulder bones.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Hettangian stage of the Lower Lias near Rugby, Warwickshire, England, dating to the dawn of the Jurassic.","Its skull was elongated and narrow, measuring nearly twice the length of its neck, a transitional condition between basal sauropterygians and derived pliosaurs.","Possessed large, forward-pointing premaxillary fangs that intermeshed with lower dentary teeth to trap swift pelagic fish.","Its pectoral and pelvic girdles formed broad, expanded ventral plates that anchored massive adductor musculature for powerful flipper downstrokes."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Macroplata tenuiceps description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macroplata"}]

name: Peloneustes
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation of England.
• Described by Richard Lydekker in 1889.
• The name translates roughly to mud swimmer.
• Known from numerous specimens.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Oxford Clay of Peterborough, England, measuring roughly 3 meters in total body length.","A relatively small, gracile pliosaurid possessing an elongated, slender rostrum and reinforced mandibular symphysis.","Unlike the giant macropredatory pliosaurs, its dentition consisted of numerous blunt, circular teeth specialized for capturing hard-shelled ammonites and belemnites.","Fossil stomach contents consistently yield thousands of chitinous cephalopod hooklets, confirming an obligate teuthophagous (squid-eating) diet."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Peloneustes philarchus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peloneustes"}]

name: Pliosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in the Kimmeridge Clay Formation of England.
• Described by Richard Owen in 1841.
• It is the type genus for the entire group of short-necked plesiosaurs.
• The famous Predator X was eventually classified as a species of Pliosaurus.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Kimmeridge Clay Formation of England, serving as the foundational type species of the clade Pliosauroidea.","Possessed an immense skull over 1.5 to 2 meters in length, armed with trihedral (three-sided) cross-section teeth designed to puncture thick marine reptile bone.","Biomechanical bite force simulations estimate a jaw-closing force exceeding 45,000 newtons, among the most powerful bites in evolutionary history.","Its four colossal flippers were hydrodynamically optimized to execute high-speed ambush attacks against giant ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs."]

name: Simolestes
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation of England in the 19th century.
• Described by Charles William Andrews in 1909.
• Name means snub-nosed thief.
• A very complete skeleton was found in a brick pit in Peterborough.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Middle Jurassic Oxford Clay of England, measuring roughly 4 to 5 meters in total length.","Possessed a distinctively short, broad, blunt skull with an expanded rosette of massive, round crushing teeth at the tip of the jaws.","Its reinforced jaw symphysis and deep temporal arcade were designed to withstand extreme torsional loads while tearing apart armored marine prey.","Fossil remains of giant marine crocodiles (Metriorhynchus) have been recovered bearing puncture marks matching Simolestes dentition."]

name: Temnodontosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by Mary Anning in Lyme Regis, England.
• Described by Richard Lydekker in 1889.
• The first ichthyosaur skull ever found belonged to this genus.
• Name means cutting-tooth lizard.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered by Mary and Joseph Anning in 1811 at Lyme Regis, Dorset, England, measuring up to 9 to 10 meters in total body length.","One of the largest apex marine predators of the Early Jurassic, possessing an enormous skull armed with robust, pointed, enamel-fluted teeth.","Fossil gut contents reveal that Temnodontosaurus actively preyed on other marine reptiles, including complete skeletons of the smaller ichthyosaur Stenopterygius.","Its massive eyes measured over 20 centimeters in diameter, providing acute low-light vision for hunting in deep oceanic waters."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Temnodontosaurus platyodon description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temnodontosaurus"}]

name: Excalibosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Lower Lias of Somerset, England, in 1984.
• Described by Christopher McGowan in 1986.
• Named after Excalibur, King Arthur legendary sword.
• Known from a nearly complete skeleton.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Lower Jurassic Blue Lias near Lilstock, Somerset, England, named after King Arthur's legendary sword 'Excalibur'.","Exhibited extreme jaw asymmetry: its upper jaw (rostrum) projected forward nearly three times the length of its lower jaw, forming a long, slender sword-like bill.","Possessed small, delicate teeth lining the upper rostrum, which it used to slash through shoals of fish in a manner identical to modern swordfish and sawfish.","Phylogenetically positioned within Leptonectidae, illustrating specialized hydrodynamic and prey-capture adaptations among Early Jurassic ichthyosaurs."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Excalibosaurus costini description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibosaurus"}]

name: Morganucodon
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in limestone fissures in Glamorgan, Wales, in 1941.
• Described by Walter Kühne in 1949.
• Its name means Glamorgan tooth.
• Thousands of isolated teeth and bones have since been found.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in Late Triassic to Early Jurassic fissure fills of Glamorgan, Wales, and Yunnan, China, measuring roughly 10 centimeters in length.","A foundational mammaliaform possessing a revolutionary 'double jaw joint', retaining the ancient reptilian articular-quadrate joint alongside the mammalian dentary-squamosal joint.","Possessed precise, diphyodont tooth replacement (a single baby tooth set followed by adult teeth), a definitive mammalian diagnostic trait.","Endocasts indicate an enlarged olfactory bulb and neocortex, driven by a nocturnal, insectivorous lifestyle requiring acute scent and sensitive hearing."]

name: Castorocauda
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Daohugou Beds of Inner Mongolia, China, in 2004.
• Described by Qiang Ji and colleagues in 2006.
• Preserved remarkably detailed impressions of hair and soft tissue.
• Name means beaver tail.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Middle Jurassic Daohugou Beds of Inner Mongolia, China, dating to roughly 164 million years ago.","Measuring over 42 centimeters in length and weighing an estimated 800 grams, Castorocauda was the largest known Jurassic mammaliaform.","Pristine fossil preservation reveals a broad, scaly, paddle-like tail identical to a modern beaver, webbed hind feet, and a dense, waterproof double-layer pelt.","Its multi-cusped, recurved teeth were specialized for grasping aquatic fish, completely overturning the idea that Mesozoic mammals were exclusively tiny terrestrial insectivores."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Castorocauda lutrasimilis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castorocauda"}]

name: Volaticotherium
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Daohugou Beds of Inner Mongolia, China.
• Described by Jin Meng and colleagues in 2006.
• The fossil excellently preserved a large gliding membrane.
• Name means ancient gliding beast.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Daohugou Beds of Ningcheng County, Inner Mongolia, China, dating to roughly 164 Ma.","Preserved with an extensive, fur-covered flight membrane (patagium) stretching between its forelimbs and hindlimbs, revealing powered or gliding flight in Jurassic mammaliaforms.","Preceded the evolution of modern flying squirrels and colugos by at least 100 million years, showcasing radical ecological divergence.","Possessed specialized shearing teeth designed for consuming hard-shelled beetles and cicadas caught while gliding between canopy trees."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Volaticotherium antiquum description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volaticotherium"}]

name: Fruitafossor
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Morrison Formation of Colorado, USA, in 2005.
• Described by Zhe-Xi Luo and John Wible.
• Named after the town of Fruita, Colorado, and fossor meaning digger.
• Nicknamed Popeye due to its massive arm bones.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Upper Jurassic Morrison Formation near Fruita, Colorado, measuring roughly 15 centimeters in total length.","Possessed hyper-developed, spade-like forelimbs with an enlarged olecranon process, displaying specialized scratch-digging adaptations identical to modern armadillos and anteaters.","Its teeth were unique among Mesozoic mammals: single-rooted, tubular, open-rooted pegs that lacked enamel and grew continuously throughout life.","Represents the earliest known specialized myrmecophagous (termite- and ant-eating) fossorial mammal in the fossil record."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Fruitafossor windscheffeli description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fruitafossor"}]

name: Juramaia
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/15/Juramaia_NT.jpg?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original","type":"art","credit":"Nobu Tamura http://paleoexhibit.blogspot.com/ http://spinops.blogspot.com/ http://www.palaeocritti.com (CC BY-SA 3.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AJuramaia%20NT.jpg"},{"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-media/242-Juramaia.png","type":"habitat_scene","credit":"Life reconstruction illustration","sourceUrl":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d7/Juramaia_NT.png"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation of Liaoning, China.
• Described by Zhe-Xi Luo and colleagues in 2011.
• The fossil preserves a nearly complete skull and skeleton with soft tissue traces.
• Name means Jurassic mother from China.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation of Liaoning Province, China, dating to approximately 160 million years ago.","Represents the geologically oldest known eutherian (placental mammal ancestor), pushing back the placental-marsupial divergence by 35 million years.","Preserved with an articulated skeleton displaying specialized forepaw and wrist anatomy adapted for climbing trees (arboreal locomotion).","Possessed a tribosphenic molar dentition and three premolars/three molars, characteristic of ancestral placental dental formulas."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Juramaia sinensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juramaia"}]

name: Agilodocodon
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation in Inner Mongolia, China.
• Described by Qing-Jin Meng and colleagues in 2015.
• Represented by an incredibly well-preserved skeleton.
• Name means agile docodont.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Middle Jurassic Tiaojishan Formation of Inner Mongolia, China, dating to roughly 165 Ma.","Possessed curved, sharp claws and flexible, mobile ankle and wrist joints adapted for rapid, agile tree-climbing (scansorial locomotion).","Its spade-like front incisors show microscopic wear facets identical to modern gum-feeding marmosets, used to gouge tree bark to feed on plant sap and resin.","Demonstrates that Mesozoic docodonts diversified into complex ecological niches including arboreal sap-feeders, aquatic swimmers, and subterranean diggers."]

name: Giganotosaurus
dietDetails: Apex predator
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1993 by Rubén Darío Carolini in Patagonia, Argentina.
• Formally named Giganotosaurus carolinii in 1995 by Coria and Salgado.
• Additional fragments of a potentially larger individual were found in later years.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Candeleros Formation of Patagonia, Giganotosaurus measured an estimated 12.2 to 13 meters in length, rivaling Tyrannosaurus in overall body length.","Its skull measured over 1.6 meters in length, armed with serrated, compressed teeth that functioned like butcher's blades to slice flesh and cause massive hemorrhaging.","Finite element analysis reveals high torsional and shearing resistance in its fused mandibular symphysis, built to withstand violent lateral jerking against giant sauropods.","Histological analysis of the holotype femur indicates that Giganotosaurus attained adult size within approximately 15 to 20 years, experiencing explosive growth rates."]

name: Deinonychus
dietDetails: Pack hunter
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1931 by Barnum Brown in Montana.
• John Ostrom redefined our understanding of dinosaurs by describing it in 1969.
• Ostrom's study of Deinonychus sparked the 'Dinosaur Renaissance'.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered by John Ostrom in 1964 in the Cloverly Formation of Montana, Deinonychus sparked the modern 'Dinosaur Renaissance' by proving dinosaurs were active, warm-blooded animals.","Possessed a hyper-extensible second toe armed with a 12-centimeter recurved sickle claw (falciform ungual), used for pinning prey and gripping flesh while climbing.","Its stiffened tail was reinforced by hyper-elongated vertebral prezygapophyses and ossified chevrons, acting as a dynamic gyroscopic counterbalance during high-speed leaps.","Direct associations with the ornithopod Tenontosaurus in multiple quarries provide compelling evidence of coordinated pack hunting or aggressive gregarious feeding."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Deinonychus antirrhopus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deinonychus"}]

name: Albertosaurus
dietDetails: Apex predator
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1884 by Joseph Burr Tyrrell in Alberta, Canada.
• Named Albertosaurus in 1905 by Henry Fairfield Osborn.
• A massive bonebed containing over 20 individuals was found in 1910.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered along the Red Deer River in Alberta, Canada, by Joseph B. Tyrrell in 1884, serving as the foundational genus of Albertosaurinae.","The famous Dry Island Buffalo Jump bonebed yielded at least 26 distinct individuals, offering unprecedented statistical evidence of pack living and gregarious social hierarchy.","Possessed longer, more gracile hindlimbs than Tyrannosaurus, with an arctometatarsalian foot structure that made it a faster, more cursorial pursuer of hadrosaurs.","Cranial scans reveal well-developed olfactory bulbs and acute stereoscopic vision, optimized for coordinated pursuit hunting across open Late Cretaceous floodplains."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Albertosaurus sarcophagus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albertosaurus"}]

name: Utahraptor
dietDetails: Large prey
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1991 by a team led by James Kirkland in Utah.
• Officially named Utahraptor ostrommaysi in 1993.
• Additional specimens have since been found trapped in a potential quicksand predator trap.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Yellow Cat Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah, measuring roughly 5 to 7 meters in length and weighing over 300 to 500 kilograms.","Represents the largest known dromaeosaurid dinosaur, possessing a massive, 24-centimeter sickle claw on its second pedal digit supported by robust, stocky hindlimbs.","Unlike gracile dromaeosaurs that relied on high-speed cursorial sprinting, Utahraptor was an ambush bruiser with thickened bones built for wrestling large iguanodonts.","A colossal 9-metric-ton fossil 'quicksand block' excavated in Utah contains an adult and multiple juvenile Utahraptors preserved together alongside iguanodont prey."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Utahraptor ostrommaysi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utahraptor"}]

name: Oviraptor
dietDetails: Opportunist
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1923 by George Olsen during an expedition to Mongolia.
• Named 'egg thief' because the first fossil was found atop a clutch of eggs.
• Later discoveries proved the eggs belonged to Oviraptor itself, and it was brooding them.
interestingFacts: ["Originally discovered in 1924 atop a nest of fossilized eggs and named 'egg thief' under the mistaken assumption it was stealing Protoceratops eggs.","Excavations in the 1990s revealed an oviraptorid embryo preserved inside an identical egg, proving the animal died while faithfully brooding its own clutch.","Its skull was short, deep, and completely toothless, equipped with a powerful keratinous beak powered by hypertrophied jaw adductor muscles to crack tough seeds and shells.","Possessed a highly pneumatic skull roof and an avian-style furcula (wishbone), illustrating the intimate evolutionary kinship between maniraptorans and birds."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Oviraptor philoceratops description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oviraptor"}]

name: Majungasaurus
dietDetails: Apex predator
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1896 by a French military officer in Madagascar.
• Originally named Megalosaurus crenatissimus by Charles Depéret in 1896.
• A complete skull discovered in 1996 clarified its classification as an abelisaurid.
interestingFacts: ["The undisputed apex predator of Late Cretaceous Madagascar's Maevarano Formation, measuring roughly 6 to 7 meters in body length.","Bone surfaces belonging to Majungasaurus frequently bear distinctive theropod feeding tooth marks with inter-denticle spacing matching only Majungasaurus itself, confirming cannibalism.","Possessed a single, rounded bony horn projecting from the fused frontal bones of its skull roof, likely used for ritualized intra-specific head-butting.","Its forelimbs were reduced to tiny, non-functional four-fingered stumps that lacked distinct wrist bones and could not flex at the elbow."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Majungasaurus crenatissimus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majungasaurus"}]

name: Baryonyx
dietDetails: Piscivore
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1983 by amateur fossil hunter William Walker in Surrey, England.
• Described in 1986 by Alan Charig and Angela Milner.
• The holotype specimen included fish scales in its stomach region.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in 1983 by amateur collector William Walker in Surrey, England, within the Early Cretaceous Weald Clay Formation.","Possessed a massive, 31-centimeter curved claw on its first manual digit (thumb), which it used to gaff fish from river currents like a modern grizzly bear.","Its elongated, gavial-like snout bore a spoon-shaped terminal rosette lined with 96 finely serrated, sub-conical teeth tailored for gripping slippery fish.","Fossilized stomach contents preserved the acid-etched scales and bones of the Cretaceous teleost fish Lepidotes alongside partially digested juvenile Iguanodon bones."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Baryonyx walkeri description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baryonyx"}]

name: Acrocanthosaurus
dietDetails: Apex predator
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the early 1940s in Oklahoma, USA.
• Named Acrocanthosaurus atokensis in 1950 by Stovall and Langston.
• A nearly complete skeleton 'Fran' was discovered in the 1990s.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Early Cretaceous Antlers and Twin Mountains Formations of Oklahoma and Texas, reaching lengths of over 11.5 meters.","Characterized by hyper-elongated neural spines on its cervical, dorsal, and caudal vertebrae that rose up to 2.5 times the height of the vertebral centra.","These neural spines anchored an immense, thick muscular ridge or fleshy hump that stabilized the spine and distributed mechanical loads when tackling large sauropods.","The famed Paluxy River trackway in Texas preserves fossilized footprints widely attributed to an Acrocanthosaurus stalking a herd of sauropods across a tidal mudflat."]

name: Dromaeosaurus
dietDetails: Small prey
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1914 by Barnum Brown in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta.
• Named by Brown and Matthew in 1922.
• The type species of the family Dromaeosauridae.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered by Barnum Brown in 1914 along the Red Deer River in Alberta, Canada, serving as the type genus of the family Dromaeosauridae.","Possessed a remarkably short, deep skull that differed sharply from the slender, elongated snouts of contemporary dromaeosaurids like Saurornitholestes.","Biomechanical jaw simulations indicate Dromaeosaurus had a crushing bite force nearly three times greater than that of Velociraptor, capable of crushing bone.","Its teeth were stout, strongly recurved, and bore heavy chisel-like denticles that resisted severe bending stresses during violent biting."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Dromaeosaurus albertensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dromaeosaurus"}]

name: Troodon
dietDetails: Small prey
discoveryHistory:
• A single tooth was discovered in 1856 by Ferdinand Vandeveer Hayden.
• Named by Joseph Leidy in 1856, making it one of the first dinosaurs named in North America.
• The genus has been considered a 'wastebasket taxon' due to confusing fossil fragments.
interestingFacts: ["Historically described by Joseph Leidy in 1856 based on a single serrated tooth, Troodon became the archetypal symbol of Mesozoic dinosaurian intelligence.","Possessed the highest encephalization quotient (brain-to-body mass ratio) of any non-avian dinosaur, with enlarged cerebrums and expansive optic lobes.","Its large, forward-facing orbits provided a high degree of binocular vision and stereoscopic depth perception for hunting small mammals and reptiles at twilight.","Recent taxonomic revisions have split classic 'Troodon' material into distinct genera (such as Stenonychosaurus and Latenivenatrix) due to subtle cranial and pelvic variations."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Troodon formosus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troodon"}]

name: Gorgosaurus
dietDetails: Apex predator
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1913 by Charles M. Sternberg in Alberta, Canada.
• Named by Lawrence Lambe in 1914.
• Over 20 skeletons have been found, making it one of the best-represented tyrannosaurids.
interestingFacts: ["A fleet-footed albertosaurine tyrannosaurid from the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada, known from dozens of complete skeletons.","Possessed long, slender metatarsals and a fused arctometatarsalian foot structure, making it one of the fastest cursorial apex predators of the Late Cretaceous.","A spectacular 2023 juvenile Gorgosaurus fossil was found with the articulated hind legs of two yearling caenagnathid dinosaurs (Citipes) preserved in its stomach cavity.","This sensational stomach-content discovery provided direct physical proof that tyrannosaurids shifted dietary niches from fast small game as juveniles to giant ceratopsians as adults."]

name: Daspletosaurus
dietDetails: Apex predator
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1921 by Charles Mortram Sternberg in Alberta.
• Dale Russell recognized it as a distinct genus and named it in 1970.
• Some specimens show bite marks from other tyrannosaurs.
interestingFacts: ["A massive, robust tyrannosaurine from Alberta, Canada, that lived alongside the more gracile and agile albertosaurine Gorgosaurus.","Possessed a heavily reinforced skull with thickened postorbital bones and robust ziphodont teeth capable of puncturing through thick ceratopsian bone and armor.","Fossil skulls frequently exhibit unhealed and healed bite marks inflicted by other tyrannosaurs, documenting fierce intra-specific territorial battles and face-biting.","Endocranial reconstructions reveal an extraordinarily acute sense of smell, with massive olfactory tracts extending forward from the cerebral hemispheres."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Daspletosaurus torosus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daspletosaurus"}]

name: Styracosaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• The first skull was collected in 1913 by Charles H. Sternberg in Alberta.
• Named by Lawrence Lambe in 1913.
• Bonebeds suggest it lived in massive herds.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada, characterized by one of the most spectacular cranial ornamentations in Dinosauria.","Its parietosquamosal frill bore four to six long, sharp, backward-projecting spikes measuring up to 60 centimeters in length.","The nasal bone was crowned with a massive, straight nose horn that reached nearly 60 centimeters in length and was sheathed in tough keratin.","Enormous monospecific bonebeds containing hundreds of individuals indicate that Styracosaurus lived and migrated in massive, socially coordinated herds."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Styracosaurus albertensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Styracosaurus"}]

name: Pachyrhinosaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1946 by Charles M. Sternberg in Alberta, Canada.
• Described and named in 1950.
• The Pipestone Creek bonebed revealed hundreds of individuals.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Pipestone Creek bonebed in Alberta, Canada, where thousands of disarticulated bones representing dozens of individuals were recovered.","Instead of a sharp nasal horn, Pachyrhinosaurus bore an enormous, flattened, rugose bony mass known as a nasal boss, which supported a thick keratinous battering ram.","Its frill featured a pair of curved, forward-pointing hook-like spikes on the upper midline and a small, horn-like unicorn spike in the center of the forehead.","Microscopic bone histology suggests that the cranial boss was highly vascularized and actively remodeled during sexual maturity for display and flank-butting."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Pachyrhinosaurus lakustai description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pachyrhinosaurus"}]

name: Centrosaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered by Lawrence Lambe in 1904 in Alberta, Canada.
• Lambe named the genus that same year based on incomplete remains.
• Enormous bonebeds in Dinosaur Provincial Park have yielded thousands of bones.
interestingFacts: ["One of the most common ceratopsians recovered from the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, known from dense bonebeds containing thousands of specimens.","Possessed a single, large nasal horn that curved forward or backward depending on maturity and individual variation, paired with forward-curving hooks on its frill.","Its deep, robust jaws housed continuous shearing dental batteries consisting of hundreds of interlocking teeth that replaced worn crowns continuously.","The massive Hildegard bonebed preserves an entire herd of Centrosaurus that drowned simultaneously while attempting to cross a swollen, flooding tropical river."]

name: Chasmosaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• First remains found in 1898 by Lawrence Lambe.
• Formally named by Lambe in 1914.
• Multiple species have been identified from the Dinosaur Park Formation.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada, distinguished by an extraordinarily expansive, heart-shaped neck frill.","Its parietal-squamosal frill accounted for nearly half the total skull length, perforated by enormous fenestrae (openings) that lightened its display surface.","Spectacular fossil specimens preserve pristine skin impressions displaying a mosaic of large, multi-faceted polygon scales bordered by smaller circular scales.","Possessed a relatively short nasal horn and two small brow horns, relying primarily on its brightly colored, vascularized frill for intra-specific signaling."]

name: Psittacosaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/01/Psittacosaurus_%28Riha2006%29.jpg?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original","type":"art","credit":"The original uploader was Pavel.Riha.CB at English Wikipedia.\n\n(Original text: Pavel Riha) (CC BY-SA 3.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3APsittacosaurus%20(Riha2006).jpg"},{"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-media/470-Psittacosaurus.jpg","type":"fossil_specimen","credit":"Life reconstruction illustration","sourceUrl":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b2/Psittacosaurus.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1922 by the American Museum of Natural History expedition to Mongolia.
• Named by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1923.
• Hundreds of complete skeletons have been found, making it one of the most studied dinosaurs.
interestingFacts: ["One of the most abundant and well-studied dinosaurs in the fossil record, with over 1,000 articulated skeletons excavated from Cretaceous beds of East Asia.","Possessed an upright, obligate bipedal stance and a parrot-like crushing beak powered by deep cheek muscles to break open tough seeds and nuts.","A world-famous fossil specimen from Liaoning, China, preserves a dense brush of long, stiff, tubular bristles (integumentary appendages) running down the top of its tail.","Spectacular ultraviolet and laser-stimulated fluorescence imaging revealed fossilized countershading camouflage, with a dark dorsal surface and pale ventral belly."]

name: Pentaceratops
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1921 by Charles H. Sternberg in the San Juan Basin, New Mexico.
• Named by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1923.
• A massive skull was discovered in 1941, one of the largest of any terrestrial animal.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Kirtland Formation of the San Juan Basin in New Mexico, measuring roughly 6 to 7 meters in total length.","Its name means 'five-horned face', referencing its prominent nose horn, two forward-curving brow horns, and two sharply flared jugal cheek spikes.","Possessed one of the largest skulls of any land animal, with an immense, rectangular neck frill that reached nearly 2.3 to 3 meters in total vertical height.","Its broad frill bore small, scalloped osteoderms (epoccipitals) along the margin, serving as an intimidating visual billboard to rivals and predators."]

name: Diabloceratops
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• The first skull was found in 2002 by Don DeBlieux in Utah's Wahweap Formation.
• Described and named by James Kirkland and colleagues in 2010.
• Represents one of the oldest known centrosaurine ceratopsids.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Wahweap Formation of Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument in southern Utah, dating to ~79 million years ago.","One of the most basal known centrosaurines, distinguished by a pair of long, curved, devil-like spikes rising upward from the top of its neck frill.","Possessed unusually long, slender supraorbital (brow) horns for a centrosaurine, retaining the primitive horn configuration seen in basal chasmosaurines.","Its deep snout was equipped with a sharp, keratinous cropping beak, adapted for browsing tough, woody riparian shrubs and palm fronds."]

name: Kosmoceratops
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Found in 2006 by a volunteer in the Kaiparowits Formation of Utah.
• Formally named by Scott Sampson and colleagues in 2010.
• Its discovery shed light on dinosaur endemism in Late Cretaceous North America.
interestingFacts: ["The most decorated and ornate ceratopsian dinosaur ever discovered, bearing an extraordinary total of 15 individual horns and horn-like processes across its skull—more cranial weaponry and display structures than any other known non-avian dinosaur.","Its 15 cranial horns break down with morphological precision: 1 blade-like nasal horn above the snout, 2 pointed postorbital brow horns curving outward over the eyes, 2 laterally projecting jugal (cheek) horns, and exactly 10 distinct epioccipital and epiparietal horns ringing the dorsal margin of its parietal frill.","Eight of the 10 frill horns curve dramatically forward and downward over the forehead like an elaborate decorative fringe of bangs, while the outermost two curve laterally, an anatomical orientation useless for combat but exquisitely evolved for visual socio-sexual display.","Discovered in 2006 by volunteer Scott Richardson in the Kaiparowits Formation of southern Utah, living on the isolated greenhouse island continent of Laramidia approximately 76 million years ago."]
sources: [{"citation":"Sampson, S. D., Loewen, M. A., Farke, A. A., Roberts, E. M., Forster, C. A., Smith, J. A., & Titus, A. L. (2010). New horned dinosaurs from Utah provide evidence for intracontinental dinosaur endemism. PLoS ONE, 5(9), e12292.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0012292"}]

name: Zuniceratops
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1996 by eight-year-old Christopher James Wolfe in New Mexico.
• Described and named by Douglas Wolfe and James Kirkland in 1998.
• Provides a crucial evolutionary link between earlier ceratopsians and later giants.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Moreno Hill Formation of Catron County, New Mexico, by eight-year-old Christopher Wolfe in 1998.","Represents the earliest known North American ceratopsian to possess prominent supraorbital (brow) horns, living roughly 91 million years ago.","Morphologically bridges the evolutionary gap between small Asian ceratopsians (like Protoceratops) and the colossal multi-ton Ceratopsidae.","Fossil bonebeds indicate that Zuniceratops lived in family groups that grazed along coastal floodplain swamps bordering the Western Interior Seaway."]

name: Sinoceratops
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2008 in the Shandong province of China.
• Described by paleontologist Xu Xing and colleagues in 2010.
• The first ceratopsid dinosaur ever found outside of North America.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Xingezhuang Formation of Shandong Province, China, representing the first definitive ceratopsid dinosaur discovered outside North America.","A basal centrosaurine measuring roughly 6 meters in length and weighing over 2 metric tons, with an immensely thickened nasal horn base.","Its parietosquamosal frill featured a distinct row of forward-curving, horn-like epiparietal hooks running across the top margin.","Its discovery proved that advanced ceratopsids migrated across the Beringian land bridge and successfully colonized Late Cretaceous Asian ecosystems."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Sinoceratops zhuchengensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinoceratops"}]

name: Einiosaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1985 by Jack Horner in the Two Medicine Formation of Montana.
• Named by Scott Sampson in 1995.
• Found in low-diversity bonebeds, indicating it lived in herds.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Two Medicine Formation of Montana, celebrated for its unique, forward-curving, hook-like nasal horn.","The nasal horn curved strongly downward and forward over the front of the beak, functioning as a ritualized wrestling hook rather than an impaling weapon.","Its parietosquamosal frill bore a pair of large, backward-pointing spikes (epiparietals) that projected straight from the top corners.","Represents a key intermediate transitional evolutionary stage linking primitive centrosaurines like Centrosaurus to derived forms like Achelousaurus."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Einiosaurus procurvicornis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einiosaurus"}]

name: Achelousaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1987 by a team led by Jack Horner in Montana.
• Named by Scott Sampson in 1995 alongside Einiosaurus.
• Represents an evolutionary transition between Einiosaurus and Pachyrhinosaurus.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Upper Cretaceous Two Medicine Formation of Montana, named in honor of paleontologist Jack Horner.","Lacked true pointed horns, possessing instead heavily rugose, flattened bony pads (bosses) over both the snout and orbital regions.","Its neck frill retained two prominent, straight, backward-directed spikes extending from the posterior parietal margin.","Represents an exquisite example of anagenesis (lineage evolution without branching), directly descended from Einiosaurus and ancestral to Pachyrhinosaurus."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Achelousaurus horneri description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achelousaurus"}]

name: Nasutoceratops
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2006 in the Kaiparowits Formation of Utah.
• Described by Scott Sampson and colleagues in 2013.
• Added to the growing list of unique dinosaurs from the region.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Kaiparowits Formation of southern Utah, dating to the late Campanian (~75.5 million years ago).","Possessed extraordinarily long, forward-curving brow horns that extended almost horizontally over its snout, resembling modern cattle.","Its snout was exceptionally deep and round, with an enlarged pneumatic nasal cavity that comprised over 75% of total pre-orbital skull length.","Its short, round neck frill lacked large spikes, relying instead on its bull-like horns and deep snout profile for visual display and sparring."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Nasutoceratops titusi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasutoceratops"}]

name: Edmontosaurus
dietDetails: Browser
discoveryHistory:
• First remains were found in the late 19th century during the Bone Wars.
• Lawrence Lambe named the genus Edmontosaurus in 1917.
• Some of the best-preserved dinosaur mummies belong to this genus.
interestingFacts: ["One of the largest hadrosaurids, reaching lengths of up to 12 to 15 meters and an estimated weight exceeding 9 metric tons.","Sensational 'mummy' specimens (such as AMNH 5060 and 'Dakota') preserve fossilized skin, muscle envelopes, hoof-like keratinous forefoot mitts, and soft-tissue fleshy combs atop the head.","Housed a continuous dental battery containing over 1,000 tightly interlocking teeth that operated as an efficient grinding mill for tough conifer needles and twigs.","Taphonomic evidence demonstrates that giant packs of Edmontosaurus formed the primary prey base for adult Tyrannosaurus rex across western North America."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Edmontosaurus annectens description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmontosaurus"}]

name: Corythosaurus
dietDetails: Browser
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e3/Corythosaurus_stebingeri.png","type":"art","credit":"Connor Ashbridge (CC0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Corythosaurus_stebingeri.png"},{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a6/Corythosaurus_casuarius_head.png?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original","type":"scientific_figure","credit":"Pavel Riha = user Pavel.Riha.CB (e-mail) (CC BY-SA 3.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ACorythosaurus%20casuarius%20head.png"},{"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-media/482-Corythosaurus.jpg","type":"museum_display","credit":"Barnum Brown (Public domain)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Corythosaurus%20restoration%20from%201916.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1912 by Barnum Brown in Alberta, Canada.
• Named Corythosaurus by Brown in 1914.
• Early specimens featured extensive skin impressions.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered along the Red Deer River in Alberta, Canada, within the Dinosaur Park Formation, named for its helmet-like cranial crest.","Its hollow, semi-circular crest was formed from expanded nasal and premaxillary bones, housing convoluted internal acoustic air passages.","Acoustic modeling indicates the crest functioned as a low-frequency resonating chamber capable of broadcasting foghorn-like vocalizations over long distances.","Several fully articulated specimens preserve extensive impressions of tuberculate skin with polygonal scales covering the flanks and tail."]

name: Maiasaura
dietDetails: Browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1978 by Marion Brandvold in the Two Medicine Formation of Montana.
• Jack Horner and Robert Makela named it Maiasaura in 1979.
• 'Egg Mountain' yielded nests, eggs, embryos, and juveniles.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered by Jack Horner in the Two Medicine Formation of Montana, Maiasaura translates to 'good mother lizard'.","Excavations at 'Egg Mountain' uncovered colonial nesting grounds, fossilized egg clutches, and nests containing altricial hatchlings with worn teeth.","The presence of worn teeth in nestling hatchlings provided the first definitive proof that dinosaurs actively brought food to their young and engaged in prolonged parental care.","Dense bonebeds containing an estimated 10,000 individuals indicate that Maiasaura traveled in colossal herds that migrated seasonally across coastal plains."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Maiasaura peeblesorum description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maiasaura"}]

name: Tsintaosaurus
dietDetails: Browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1950 in Shandong Province, China.
• C.C. Young named the genus in 1958.
• Its distinctive crest was initially thought to be an artifact of preservation.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Jingangkou Formation of Shandong Province, China, dating to the late Campanian stage (~72 Ma).","Famous for its iconic tubular cranial crest: once thought to be a unicorn-like spike, comprehensive re-examinations confirmed it formed the posterior wall of a broad hollow crest.","The hollow crest was connected directly to the nasal cavity and functioned in species recognition, olfactory enhancement, and vocal resonance.","Possessed robust, quadrupedal forelimbs and a heavy pelvic girdle, allowing it to transition effortlessly between four-legged browsing and bipedal running."]

name: Lambeosaurus
dietDetails: Browser
discoveryHistory:
• First materials collected in 1902 by Lawrence Lambe.
• William Parks named it Lambeosaurus in 1923 in honor of Lambe.
• Has had a complicated taxonomic history with many species consolidated over time.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada, serving as the foundational type genus of the subfamily Lambeosaurinae.","Possessed a distinctive hatchet-shaped cranial crest comprising a vertical anterior blade and a slender, backward-pointing posterior horn.","Exhibited pronounced sexual and ontogenetic dimorphism: adult males possessed significantly larger, more upright crests than females and juveniles.","Its tail was deep and stiffened by a crisscrossing lattice of ossified tendons, providing balance while galloping or wading across coastal floodplains."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Lambeosaurus lambei description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambeosaurus"}]

name: Ouranosaurus
dietDetails: Browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1965 by French paleontologist Philippe Taquet in Niger.
• Formally described and named in 1976.
• Found in the same geological formation as Spinosaurus.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Elrhaz Formation of Niger, dating to the Early Cretaceous (Aptian stage, ~112 million years ago).","Its dorsal vertebrae bore hyper-elongated, blade-like neural spines up to 1 meter tall, forming a high dorsal sail or thick muscular fat-storage hump.","Possessed a wide, flattened, duck-like bill followed by specialized dental batteries, optimized for harvesting tough riparian ferns, horsetails, and shrubs.","Retained a small, conical thumb spike on its first manual digit, utilized for defense against contemporary apex theropods like Suchomimus."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Ouranosaurus nigeriensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ouranosaurus"}]

name: Saurolophus
dietDetails: Browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1911 by Barnum Brown in Alberta, Canada.
• Named in 1912 by Brown.
• A second species was discovered in Mongolia in the 1940s.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Horseshoe Canyon Formation of Alberta, with a closely related giant sister species (S. angustirostris) excavated in the Nemegt Formation of Mongolia.","Possessed a solid, backward-pointing, rod-like cranial crest constructed from the nasal bones that projected over the top of the skull roof.","Pristine skin impressions demonstrate that Saurolophus bore distinct vertical stripes of large, raised limpet-shaped scales along its tail and flanks.","Proves that late hadrosaurine lineages migrated freely between East Asia and North America across the Cretaceous Beringian land bridge."]

name: Olorotitan
dietDetails: Browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1999 in the Amur Region of Far Eastern Russia.
• Named in 2003 by Pascal Godefroit and colleagues.
• Its skeleton was exceptionally complete for an Asian hadrosaur.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Tsagayan Formation of the Amur Region in far eastern Russia, dating to the latest Maastrichtian (~66 Ma).","Characterized by a unique, backward-pointing, fan-shaped cranial crest that rose vertically from the back of the skull like an inverted ax blade.","Possessed an exceptionally elongated neck comprising 18 cervical vertebrae, more than any other known hadrosaur, providing broad vertical browse reach.","Its sacrum and proximal caudal vertebrae were reinforced by additional fused bony bridges, supporting a massive body mass near the K-Pg boundary."]

name: Wiwaxia corrugata

interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Burgess Shale, Wiwaxia was a bizarre, slug-like bilaterian reaching roughly 5 centimeters in length.","Its soft body was completely covered by overlapping, ribbed organic armor scales (sclerites) alongside two parallel rows of long, upward-curving defensive spines.","Possessed a ventral feeding apparatus equipped with two to three rows of conical chitinous teeth, functioning like a primitive molluscan radula.","Microscopic examination of the sclerite surfaces revealed microscopic diffraction gratings that created an iridescent, metallic rainbow sheen in Cambrian sunlight."]
sizeNotes: Excluding spines, body length was around 5 cm.

name: Bothriolepis canadensis
dietDetails: Mud-feeder, filtering organic detritus from bottom sediments.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Miguasha, Quebec, and described by Whiteaves in 1880.
interestingFacts: ["One of the most widely distributed placoderms in Earth's history, with articulated fossils discovered in Devonian sediments across every modern continent.","Its thoracic armor was articulated to a pair of unique, jointed, hollow, bony pectoral appendages (arms) that functioned like crab-like walking flippers or sediment anchors.","Possessed specialized ventral pharyngeal pouches that some paleobiologists interpret as primitive paired lungs, allowing it to gulp atmospheric oxygen in stagnant waters.","High-resolution synchrotron imaging reveals that Bothriolepis fed by ingesting nutrient-rich mud, sifting organic detritus through a fine internal gill-raker system."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Bothriolepis canadensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bothriolepis%20canadensis"}]

name: Eusthenopteron foordi
dietDetails: Hunted smaller fishes and invertebrates in shallow waters.
discoveryHistory: Named by J.F. Whiteaves in 1881 based on Miguasha specimens.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in exceptional, three-dimensional limestone concretions in the Late Devonian Escuminac Formation of Miguasha, Quebec, Canada.","An iconic 'lobe-finned' tetrapodomorph fish that possessed the internal humerus, radius, and ulna in the forelimb, and femur, tibia, and fibula in the hindlimb.","Its skull was divided by an intracranial joint, allowing the snout to flex upward relative to the braincase during explosive lunges at prey.","Possessed teeth with complex labyrinthodont internal enamel folding, establishing the direct anatomical evolutionary transition from lobe-fins to early four-limbed tetrapods."]

name: Hylonomus lyelli
dietDetails: Fed on early insects, millipedes, and land snails.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by John William Dawson in Nova Scotia inside fossilized tree trunks in 1852.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in 1852 by Sir William Dawson preserved inside petrified lycopsid tree stumps (Sigillaria) in the Carboniferous Joggins Fossil Cliffs of Nova Scotia.","Represents the earliest confirmed amniote in the fossil record (~315 Ma), having evolved the revolutionary cleidoic (shelled) egg that freed vertebrates from aquatic reproduction.","Its skull lacked temporal fenestrae (anapsid condition) and was armed with small, sharp, peg-like teeth adapted for piercing the chitinous armor of Carboniferous millipedes and insects.","Possessed slender, lizard-like proportions with clawed digits and flexible wrist joints, allowing agile scurrying across Carboniferous coal swamp floors."]
sizeNotes: Total length including tail was about 20 centimeters.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Hylonomus lyelli description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hylonomus%20lyelli"}]

name: Diplocaulus magnicornis
dietDetails: Preyed on fish, insects, and smaller amphibians.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6b/Diplocaulusdb21.jpg?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original","type":"art","credit":"Original uploader was ДиБгд at ru.wikipedia (Public domain)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ADiplocaulusdb21.jpg"},{"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-media/572-Diplocaulus.jpg","type":"skeletal_reconstruction","credit":"Life reconstruction illustration","sourceUrl":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4f/Diplocaulus_NT_small.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory: Described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1877 from Texas.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Early Permian Red Beds of Texas, measuring roughly 1 meter in length, famous for its colossal boomerang-shaped skull.","The massive lateral horns of its skull were formed by hyper-elongated tabular and squamosal bones, functioning as dynamic hydrodynamic lifting hydrofoils.","Biomechanical flume tests reveal that water flowing across the boomerang skull generated substantial vertical lift, allowing Diplocaulus to shoot upward to ambush prey.","Its nostrils were located on the dorsal surface of the head, and its eyes faced straight upward, indicating a benthic ambush predator lying concealed in river mud."]
sizeNotes: Reached up to 1 meter in length; flat-bodied.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Diplocaulus magnicornis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplocaulus%20magnicornis"}]

name: Estemmenosuchus uralensis
dietDetails: Likely herbivore-leaning omnivore eating tough leaves, tubers, and carrion.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Perm Krai, Russia, in 1960.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Middle Permian Ocher Assemblage of Perm Krai, Russia, measuring roughly 3 to 4.5 meters in length and weighing over 1 metric ton.","Its massive skull was crowned by an elaborate array of bony horns, including moose-like upward flaring antlers on the frontals and bulging lateral bosses on the cheeks.","Possessed an eclectic heterodont dentition featuring sharp, conical incisors, colossal predatory canine tusks, and small, serrated postcanine teeth for grinding plants.","Histological analysis of exceptional Russian specimens preserves impressions of smooth, glandular skin that lacked reptilian scales, foreshadowing synapsid glandular skin."]
sizeNotes: Massive bull-like build up to 4 meters long.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Estemmenosuchus uralensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estemmenosuchus%20uralensis"}]

name: Andrewsarchus mongoliensis
dietDetails: Likely scavenger and predator, crushing bones and eating turtles.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by Kan Chuen Pao during Roy Chapman Andrews' Central Asiatic Expedition in 1923.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in 1923 by Kan Chuen Pao during Roy Chapman Andrews' American Museum of Natural History expedition to the Irdin Manha Formation of Inner Mongolia.","The holotype skull measures an astonishing 83 centimeters in length and 56 centimeters wide, making it one of the largest terrestrial carnivorous mammals known.","Historically classified as a mesonychid, recent phylogenetic analyses place Andrewsarchus as a basal artiodactyl, closely related to entelodonts ('hell pigs') and hippos.","Its blunt, robust premolars and heavily worn molars were built for immense crushing power, capable of splintering thick bone, crushing turtles, and tearing carrion."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Andrewsarchus mongoliensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrewsarchus%20mongoliensis"}]

name: Uintatherium anceps
dietDetails: Browsed on soft forest foliage and leaves.
discoveryHistory: Discovered during the bone wars and described by Leidy, Marsh, and Cope.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Middle Eocene Bridger Formation of Wyoming and Utah, Uintatherium was a colossal, rhinoceros-sized dinoceratan herbivore.","Its bizarre skull featured three distinct pairs of knobby, skin-covered bony ossicones (horns) on the snout, forehead, and cheeks, alongside a deep concave cranial bowl.","Adult males possessed enormous, saber-like upper canine tusks that were protected when the mouth was closed by deep, downturned bony flanges on the lower jaw.","Despite its 4-meter body length and 2-metric-ton bulk, its brain cavity was remarkably small, smaller than that of a modern domestic dog."]
sizeNotes: Comparable in size to a modern white rhinoceros.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Uintatherium anceps description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uintatherium%20anceps"}]

name: Paraceratherium transouralicum
dietDetails: Browsed leaves and twigs from tree canopies.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Pakistan and described by Forster-Cooper in 1911.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered throughout the Oligocene floodplains of Central Asia, Paraceratherium was the largest land mammal ever to walk the Earth, reaching 7.4 meters in length.","Stood roughly 4.8 meters tall at the shoulder with an estimated body mass of 15 to 20 metric tons, easily browsing canopy branches 7 meters above the ground.","Possessed a pair of downward-pointing, chisel-like upper incisors that worked against forward-pointing lower incisors to strip bark and shear tough desert shrubs.","Its three-toed, columnar limbs lacked collarbones (clavicles), and its cervical vertebrae were lightened by deep lateral excavations to support its elongated neck."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Paraceratherium transouralicum description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraceratherium%20transouralicum"}]

name: Titanoboa cerrejonensis
dietDetails: Preyed on giant crocodiles, turtles, and large fish.
discoveryHistory: No discovery history available.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in 2009 in the open-cast coal mines of the Cerrejón Formation in La Guajira, Colombia, dating to the middle Paleocene (~58-60 Ma).","Measuring an estimated 12.8 to 14.3 meters in length and weighing over 1.1 metric tons, Titanoboa is the largest snake ever documented in Earth's history.","Calculations based on poikilothermic reptile metabolic limits indicate that supporting a snake of Titanoboa's mass required an equatorial mean annual temperature of 30°C to 34°C.","Its tooth anatomy and skull structure indicate that Titanoboa was specialized for hunting giant aquatic prey, constricting colossal dyrosaurid crocodiles and giant pelomedusid turtles."]
sizeNotes: Reached up to 12.8 meters (42 ft) in length and weighed 1.1 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Titanoboa cerrejonensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanoboa%20cerrejonensis"}]

name: Moeritherium lyonsi
dietDetails: Browsed aquatic plants and soft vegetation along lake margins.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by Charles William Andrews in Egypt in 1901.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene Qasr el Sagha Formation of the Fayum Depression, Egypt, measuring roughly 70 centimeters tall and 2 meters long.","A foundational stem-proboscidean that possessed an amphibious, tapir-like or pygmy-hippo-like semi-aquatic ecology in lush mangrove swamps.","Its upper and lower second incisors were enlarged into incipient, chisel-like tusks, while its elongated upper lip and nose formed a prehensile, mobile snout.","Stable oxygen isotope values in its tooth enamel match those of fully aquatic mammals, confirming that ancestral elephants spent most of their lives submerged in water."]
sizeNotes: Stood about 70 cm tall at the shoulder.

name: Stygimoloch
dietDetails: Browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the 19th or 20th century.
• Holotype found in Cretaceous fossil beds.
• Named Stygimoloch by paleontologists after careful study.
• Subsequent discoveries expanded our understanding of its anatomy.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Hell Creek Formation of Montana and Wyoming, dating to the latest Maastrichtian stage (~66 million years ago).","Characterized by a narrow, reduced frontoparietal dome surrounded by a dramatic cluster of three to four long, horn-like spikes measuring up to 10 centimeters.","In 2009, paleontologists Jack Horner and Mark Goodwin presented extensive histological evidence proposing that Stygimoloch represents a subadult ontogenetic stage of Pachycephalosaurus.","Bone cross-sections show high levels of active cranial remodeling, where juvenile horns were reabsorbed and incorporated into the expanding adult dome as the animal matured."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Stygimoloch spinifer description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stygimoloch"}]

name: Dracorex
dietDetails: Browser

Peterson, Collin Dischler, Nicholas R. Longrich (CC BY 2.5)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pachycephalosauridae%20head%20butting.png"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the 19th or 20th century.
• Holotype found in Cretaceous fossil beds.
• Named Dracorex by paleontologists after careful study.
• Subsequent discoveries expanded our understanding of its anatomy.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Hell Creek Formation of South Dakota in 2004 by amateur collectors and named in honor of the fictional Hogwarts school from J.K. Rowling's Harry Potter books.","Possessed a completely flat skull roof that lacked a developed dome, adorned with an elaborate crown of sharp, symmetrical spikes and nodes across the squamosals.","Microscopic histological analysis of the flat skull showed open cranial sutures and juvenile vascularization, supporting its classification as the juvenile form of Pachycephalosaurus.","Possessed small, serrated premaxillary teeth and a sharp keratinous beak, specialized for browsing high-quality herbs, roots, and fruits."]

name: Rajasaurus narmadensis
dietDetails: Apex predator preying on large titanosaurian sauropods and ornithopods in Cretaceous floodplains.
discoveryHistory:
• Unearthed between 1981 and 1983 by Geological Survey of India (GSI) geologists G.N. Dwivedi and Dhananjay Mohabey near Rahioli, Gujarat.
• Excavated under the leadership of GSI paleontologist Suresh Srivastava, who recovered a nearly complete braincase and associated skeleton.
• Formally described in 2003 by a joint Indian-American team including Paul Sereno and Jeffrey A. Wilson after two decades in storage.
• Designated as the holotype GSI Type No. 19/999, providing crucial evidence of abelisaurid distribution on southern landmasses.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in 1983 by Suresh Srivastava in the Lameta Formation of Gujarat, western India, along the banks of the Narmada River; its name means 'princely lizard of Narmada'.","Possessed a prominent, rounded horn core on the midline of its skull roof formed by the fused frontal bones, utilized for intra-specific head-butting.","A formidable abelisaurid measuring roughly 7.5 to 9 meters in length, acting as the undisputed apex macropredator of the isolated Late Cretaceous Indian subcontinent.","Preyed upon the diverse titanosaurian sauropods (such as Jainosaurus and Isisaurus) that nested in immense numbers along the volcanic floodplains of the Deccan Traps."]
sizeNotes: Consensus length of 6.6 to 7.4 meters and weight of 1.5 metric tonnes, standing about 2.4 meters tall at the hip.

name: Indosuchus
dietDetails: Carnivorous predator of small to medium-sized dinosaurs.
discoveryHistory:
• Collected between 1917 and 1919 by British geologist Charles Alfred Matley near Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh.
• Formally named by German paleontologist Friedrich von Huene in 1932.
• Described in detail by Huene and Matley in a joint monograph in 1933.
• Originally classified as an allosaurid, then a tyrannosaurid, before modern analysis confirmed it as an abelisaurid.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Late Cretaceous Lameta Formation of Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh, India, by Charles Alfred Matley and described by Friedrich von Huene in 1933.","Possessed a remarkably narrow, laterally compressed skull with deep alveolar margins, specialized for delivering high-velocity slicing bites against tough sauropod hide.","Historically classified as a carnosaur or tyrannosauroid, modern cladistic analyses place Indosuchus firmly within Abelisauridae alongside Rajasaurus.","Its discovery proved that abelisaurid theropods achieved immense ecological and morphological diversity across Gondwanan landmasses before the K-Pg extinction."]
sizeNotes: Estimated to be roughly 6 to 7 meters in length and weighing 1.2 metric tonnes.

name: Vasuki
dietDetails: Ambush predator that subdued prey through constriction, likely feeding on early mammals, crocodilians, and turtles.
discoveryHistory:
• Holotype vertebrae GSI/GG/V/001–027 were originally discovered in 2005 at the Panandhro Lignite Mine in Kutch, Gujarat.
• The fossil material was initially misidentified as belonging to an extinct crocodilian and stored in the IIT Roorkee archives.
• Re-examined in 2024 by paleontologists Debajit Datta and Sunil Bajpai, who recognized it as a giant madtsoiid snake.
• Named after 'Vasuki', the mythical serpent king from Hindu cosmology, and 'indicus' to denote its geographic discovery site.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in 2024 in the Lignite Mine of Panandhro, Kutch, Gujarat, India, within the Middle Eocene Naredi Formation (~47 Ma).","Measuring an estimated 11 to 15 meters in length and weighing roughly 1 metric ton, Vasuki rivals Titanoboa as one of the largest snakes ever to exist.","Belongs to the extinct family Madtsoiidae, characterized by massive vertebrae measuring over 6 centimeters wide with complex accessory zygosphene-zygantrum joints.","Named after the mythical serpent king 'Vasuki' from Hindu cosmology who rests around the neck of Lord Shiva, celebrating India's rich paleontological heritage."]
sizeNotes: Length estimates range from 10.9 to 15.2 meters with a weight of approximately 1 metric tonne based on vertebral dimensions.

name: Sivatherium
dietDetails: Browsed on leaves, shrubs, and woody vegetation.
discoveryHistory:
• First fossils discovered in the Siwalik Hills of northern India and described in 1836 by Hugh Falconer and Captain Proby Thomas Cautley.
• The bizarre skeletal remains initially sparked intense debate and were mistakenly likened to elephants, rhinos, or oxen.
• Re-examined in 2016 through a detailed 3D skeletal reconstruction using fossils housed at the Natural History Museum in London.
• Placed within the family Giraffidae, closely related to the modern okapi.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Pliocene to Early Pleistocene Siwalik Hills of northern India and Pakistan, measuring roughly 3 meters tall at the shoulder.","A colossal, heavily built giraffid that weighed roughly 1.2 to 1.5 metric tons, making it one of the largest ruminant mammals in Earth's history.","Its skull was crowned by two pairs of massive bony ossicones: a smaller conical pair above the eyes and a gigantic, palmate, moose-like pair sweeping backward from the parietals.","Possessed robust, stocky limbs and deep cheek teeth with crenulated enamel, adapted for browsing coarse gymnosperms, acacia branches, and gritty savanna scrub."]
sizeNotes: Shoulder height of 2.2 meters, total length around 3 meters, and weight of approximately 1,246 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Sivatherium giganteum description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sivatherium"}]

name: Stegodon ganesa
dietDetails: Browser feeding on grass, leaves, and twigs in Pleistocene river plains.
discoveryHistory:
• Formally described and named in 1846 by Hugh Falconer and Proby Thomas Cautley based on fossils found in the Siwalik Hills.
• Extensive skull and tusk material has been recovered across northern India, Pakistan, and Myanmar.
• Recent excavations in 2025 recovered exceptionally preserved fossils in the Chandrapur district of Maharashtra.
• These Maharashtra fossils were found in deep riverbed sediments and dated to approximately 25,000 years ago.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Early Pleistocene Upper Siwalik formations of northern India, named after the elephant-headed Hindu deity Ganesha.","Possessed extraordinarily massive, spiraled, closely spaced tusks that reached up to 3 to 3.5 meters in length, curving outward and upward from the upper jaw.","Its massive molar teeth exhibited low-crowned enamel ridges (lamellae) shaped like roof-like gables (stegos), specialized for shearing tough bamboo and riverbank vegetation.","The legendary 1845 holotype cranium and colossal tusks housed at the Natural History Museum in London remain among the most spectacular fossil proboscideans ever unearthed."]
sizeNotes: Shoulder height of up to 4 meters, and weight estimated at around 10 metric tonnes.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Stegodon ganesa description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stegodon%20ganesa"}]

name: Shringasaurus
dietDetails: Low-browsing herbivore feeding on ferns and cycads.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Madhya Pradesh, India, and described in 2017 by Sartee Sengupta and colleagues.
interestingFacts: ["Features a pair of prominent forward-facing horns over its eyes, similar to modern ceratopsians.","Demonstrates sexual dimorphism with horns likely used in combat.","Adapted for a specialized herbivore trophic niche within its ecosystem, utilizing refined cranial mechanics to process its primary food sources.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate estimated from bone beds containing at least 7 individuals, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Estimated from bone beds containing at least 7 individuals.
sources: [{"citation":"Sengupta, S. et al. (2017). An unusual horned archosauromorph from the Middle Triassic of India. Scientific Reports 7: 8366.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-08658-8"}]

name: Gigantophis garstini
dietDetails: Apex ambush predator preying on early basal proboscideans (such as Moeritherium) and primitive artiodactyls.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 1901 by British paleontologist Charles William Andrews in the Eocene Birket Qarun Formation of the Fayum Depression in Egypt.
interestingFacts: ["For over a century until the discovery of Titanoboa in 2009, Gigantophis was considered the largest known snake to have ever existed.","Historically estimated at 9 to 10 meters, a 2004 reassessment by Jason Head et al. revised its estimated length downward to approximately 6.9 ± 0.3 meters.","Belongs to the extinct family Madtsoiidae, sharing a deep evolutionary lineage with other giant Paleogene snakes such as Vasuki and Madtsoia.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate historically estimated at 9–10m; revised in 2004 to ~6.9m, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Historically estimated at 9–10m; revised in 2004 to ~6.9m.

Geological Magazine 8(10): 436–444.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38102"},{"citation":"Head, J.J., et al. (2004).
