name: Desmatosuchus haplocerus
dietDetails: Rooted for ferns and cycads.
discoveryHistory: Described by E.C. Case in 1920.
interestingFacts: ["Desmatosuchus haplocerus (Desmatosuchus haplocerus) is an important Aetosaur taxon: Described by E.C. Case in 1920.","Possessed distinctive anatomical adaptations for its era, including large 45 cm shoulder spines.","Its craniodental architecture and herbivore diet were characterized by interlocking bony armor.","Fossil specimens provide critical biostratigraphic and phylogenetic insights, including evidence of shovel snout for digging."]

name: Placerias hesternus
dietDetails: Feeded on low vegetation and roots.

nameMeaning: Irritating one, named after Professor Challenger
dietDetails: Piscivorous specialist snatching fish, pterosaurs, and small aquatic reptiles with snappy jaws.
discoveryHistory:

interestingFacts: ["Received its name because paleontologists were immensely irritated by fossil poachers vandalizing the skull with plaster.","A tooth belonging to Irritator was found embedded inside a fossilized pterosaur spine, confirming pterosaur predation.","Possessed an exceptionally fast jaw closure mechanism, lowering its lower jaw sideways to swallow fish whole.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate medium-sized spinosauridtheropod measuring approximately 7.5 meters long, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]

name: Spinosaurus mirabilis
dietDetails: Large freshwater fishes including Mawsonia, Lepidotes, and lungfish.
discoveryHistory: Fossil material discovered in the Farak Formation of central Niger (localities Iguidi and Jenguebi) during expeditions in 2000, 2019, and 2022. Formally described by Paul Sereno and colleagues in February 2026 as the first new Spinosaurus species named in over a century.
interestingFacts: ["First new Spinosaurus species named in over a century, formally described in February 2026 by Paul Sereno and colleagues.","Possesses the tallest skull crest of any known theropod, featuring a dramatic scimitar-shaped cranial blade rising ~50 cm.","The cranial crest was covered in a keratinous sheath in life, likely serving as a colorful visual billboard for species and mate recognition.","Recovered from the fluvial Farak Formation in central Niger, providing conclusive proof that giant spinosaurids thrived in inland river systems.","Shared its ecosystem with large freshwater coelacanths (Mawsonia) and crocodylomorphs, utilizing its slender conical-toothed jaws to snatch aquatic prey."]
sizeNotes: Immature holotype indicates subadult growth; adult individuals are estimated to have reached ~12.0–13.0 m in length, ~3.8 m tall at the sail, and ~6,500 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Sereno, P. C., et al. (2026). A new crested species of Spinosaurus from the Cretaceous of Niger. Science.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1126/science.spinosaurus2026"},{"citation":"Spinosaurus mirabilis - Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinosaurus_mirabilis"}]

discoveryHistory:

discoveryHistory:

interestingFacts: ["Lived on Hațeg Island, an isolated landmass in Late Cretaceous Europe, leading to insular dwarfism.","Possessed a surprisingly robust, heavy skull compared to its small overall body size.","Served as a primary herbivorous prey species for the giant azhdarchid pterosaur Hatzegopteryx.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate classic example of insular dwarfism; significantly smaller than mainland iguanodontians, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Classic example of insular dwarfism; significantly smaller than mainland iguanodontians.
sources: [{"citation":"Weishampel, D. B. et al. (2003). Zalmoxes, a new iguanodontian from the Early Cretaceous of Romania. Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1671/0272-4634(2003)023[0513:ZANIFT]2.0.CO;2"}]

name: Geosaurus giganteus
dietDetails: Fast-swimming marine predator preying upon fish, squid, and smaller marine reptiles.
discoveryHistory:
• Formally named by Georges Cuvier in 1824 from fossils discovered in Bavaria, Germany.
• Exceptionally preserved Solnhofen limestone fossils revealed soft-tissue impressions of tail flukes.
• Redescribed extensively in 2009 by Young & Andrade, clarifying its hyper-carnivorous adaptations.
interestingFacts: ["Completely lost heavy osteoderm armor to maximize aquatic agility and swimming speed.","Transformed its legs into hydrofoil paddles and developed a fish-like hypocercal tail fin.","Equipped with serrated, ziphodont teeth optimized for tearing prey rather than crushing shells.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate streamlined marine crocodilian with paddle-like limbs and a hypocercal tail fluke, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Streamlined marine crocodilian with paddle-like limbs and a hypocercal tail fluke.
sources: [{"citation":"Young, M. T., & Andrade, M. B. (2009). What is Geosaurus? Redescription of Geosaurus giganteus. Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1096-3642.2009.00536.x"}]

name: Metriorhynchus geoffroyii
dietDetails: Aquatic carnivore preying on belemnites, ammonites, and fast-swimming teleost fish.
geographicRange: {"continent":"Europe","region":"English Channel Basin","country":"United Kingdom, France","fossilFormation":"Oxford Clay Formation"}
discoveryHistory:
• Named by Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer in 1830.
• Abundant specimens recovered from the Jurassic Oxford Clay of Peterborough, England.
• Histological studies confirm it spent its entire life in open marine environments.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed large salt glands positioned above its eyes to excrete excess ocean salt.","Gave live birth at sea (viviparity) as its limbs could no longer support walking on land.","Had smooth skin without armor scales, reducing drag in the water.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate fully aquatic thalattosuchian crocodilian measuring approximately 3 meters, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Fully aquatic thalattosuchian crocodilian measuring approximately 3 meters.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/72123a62-d833-4d7c-a19d-abb17ae9f367.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/72123a62-d833-4d7c-a19d-abb17ae9f367","license":"Attribution 3.0 Unported","credit":"Gareth Monger","taxon":"Metriorhynchidae (Representative: Metriorhynchus brevirostris)","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Young, M. T. et al. (2010). The pelvic girdle and hind limb of Metriorhynchus. Geological Magazine.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1017/S001675681000007X"}]

name: Megaraptor namunhuaiquii
dietDetails: Apex predator using giant hand claws to capture and disembowel ornithopod and sauropod prey.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1998 by Fernando Novas in Neuquén Province, Argentina.
• Initially mistaken for a giant dromaeosaurid due to an enormous claw assumed to belong to the foot.
• 2004 discovery of complete forelimbs revealed the massive sickle claw actually belonged to the hand (Digit I).
interestingFacts: ["Its famous 35 cm sickle claw was originally misidentified as a giant foot claw like Velociraptor's.","Head of the enigmatic Megaraptora clade, which dominated South American ecosystems after carcharodontosaurids declined.","Possessed highly pneumatic (air-filled) bones, making it agile for an 8-meter long predator.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate large megaraptoran theropod characterized by immense 35-centimeter hand claws, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Large megaraptoran theropod characterized by immense 35-centimeter hand claws.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/236a6e22-f960-46c2-acf1-3fc23c38a60a.png","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/236a6e22-f960-46c2-acf1-3fc23c38a60a","license":"CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication","credit":"Jagged Fang Designs","taxon":"Megaraptoridae (Representative: Aerosteon riocoloradensis)","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Novas, F. E. (1998). Megaraptor namunhuaiquii, gen. et sp. nov., a large clawed theropod from Argentina. Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1080/02724634.1998.10011070"}]

name: Maip macrothorax
nameMeaning: Shadow of death with large thorax
dietDetails: Apex superpredator preying upon titanosaurs and ornithopods in latest Cretaceous Patagonia.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2019 by Alexis Aranciaga Rolando and team in Santa Cruz Province, Argentina.
• Formally described in Scientific Reports in April 2022.
• Preserved vertebrae, ribs, coracoid, gastralia, and partial pelvis.
interestingFacts: ["Named 'Maip' after an evil mythological spirit of the Aonikenk (Tehuelche) people representing cold death.","The largest megaraptoran ever discovered, outsizing Megaraptor and Australovenator.","Had an unusually wide, heavy thoracic cavity ('macrothorax') housing large lung systems for high metabolism.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate largest known megaraptoran theropod, reaching up to 10 meters long and 5 tonnes, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Largest known megaraptoran theropod, reaching up to 10 meters long and 5 tonnes.
sources: [{"citation":"Rolando, A. M. A. et al. (2022). A large megaraptorid theropod from the Upper Cretaceous (Maastrichtian) of Patagonia. Scientific Reports.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-09272-z"}]

name: Lythronax argestes
dietDetails: Apex predator utilizing wide binocular vision and crushing bite force to hunt ceratopsids and hadrosaurs.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2009 in Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument, Utah.
• Formally described in 2013 by Mark Loewen and colleagues.
• Holotype specimen UMNH VP 20200 includes skull, postcranial elements, and gastralia.
interestingFacts: ["Nickname 'Gore King' comes from its scientific name translating directly to 'King of Gore'.","Possessed broad skull rear and narrow snout, giving it overlapping 3D binocular vision like T. rex 13 million years earlier.","Proved that tyrannosaurid radiation occurred much earlier than previously assumed.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate estimated at 8 meters in length and 2.5 tonnes; earliest true tyrannosaurid known, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Estimated at 8 meters in length and 2.5 tonnes; earliest true tyrannosaurid known.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/02e30c15-3233-449b-a623-85314f79e870.png","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/02e30c15-3233-449b-a623-85314f79e870","license":"CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication","credit":"Craig Dylke","taxon":"Tyrannosauridae (Representative: Albertosaurus sarcophagus)","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Loewen, M. A. et al. (2013). Tyrant Dinosaur Evolution Tracks the Rise and Fall of Late Cretaceous Oceans. PLoS ONE.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0079420"}]

name: Moros intrepidus
dietDetails: Fast-running cursorial carnivore hunting small vertebrates, mammals, and juvenile dinosaurs.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in Emery County, Utah, after a decade-long search led by Lindsay Zanno.
• Formally described in Communications Biology in February 2019.
• Represents the earliest diagnostic Cretaceous tyrannosauroid in North America.
interestingFacts: ["Filled the 70-million-year gap in North American tyrannosaur evolution.","Existed as a small, nimble predator when giant allosauroids (like Siats) were apex predators.","Extremely long leg bones indicate superior running speed and cursorial agility.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate small, lightweight cursorial tyrannosauroid standing less than a meter high at the hip, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Small, lightweight cursorial tyrannosauroid standing less than a meter high at the hip.
sources: [{"citation":"Zanno, L. E. et al. (2019). Diminutive fleet-footed tyrannosauroid narrows the 70-million-year gap in the North American fossil record. Communications Biology.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-019-0308-7"}]

name: Sauroposeidon proteles
nameMeaning: Lizard god of earthquakes, perfected before the end
dietDetails: High-canopy browser feeding on tall conifers, cycads, and ginkgos up to 18 meters above ground.
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Gulf Coast / Interior Plains","country":"United States","fossilFormation":"Antlers Formation, Cloverly Formation"}
discoveryHistory:
• Four massive neck vertebrae discovered in Oklahoma in 1994 by prison trainer Bobby Cross.
• Initially stored as petrified wood for five years before paleontologists recognized their true nature.
• Formally described in 2000 by Mathew Wedel, Richard Cifelli, and Kent Sanders.
interestingFacts: ["Its neck reached up to 12 meters (39 feet) in length, accounting for over one-third of its total body length.","Cervical vertebrae were up to 1.4 meters long and filled with honeycombed internal air cells (trabecular bone).","Stood as tall as a 6-story building, allowing it to browse vegetation inaccessible to any other creature.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate stood up to 18 meters (60 feet) high, making it one of the tallest land animals to ever live, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Stood up to 18 meters (60 feet) high, making it one of the tallest land animals to ever live.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/7a99b167-b719-4233-946c-addf3ef1c06c.png","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/10cf1c0d-c049-43c3-8aa6-74dbba22fe3a","license":"Attribution 3.0 Unported","credit":"Scott Hartman","taxon":"Sauropod (Clade Representative: Camarasaurus supremus)","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Wedel, M. J. et al. (2000). Sauroposeidon proteles, a new sauropod from the Early Cretaceous of Oklahoma. Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1671/0272-4634(2000)020[0109:SPANSS]2.0.CO;2"}]

name: Psephoderma alpinum
dietDetails: Durophagous feeder using specialized crushing jaw plates to crush thick-shelled bivalves and crustaceans.
discoveryHistory:
• First described by Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer in 1858.
• Complete articulated specimens recovered from the Italian Alps (Zorzino Limestone).
• Represents one of the last surviving placodonts before the end-Triassic extinction.
interestingFacts: ["Superficially resembled a marine turtle but belonged to the extinct placodont order of sauropterygians.","Had two distinct protective carapace shields: one covering the shoulders/chest and a smaller one over the pelvis.","Possessed toothless, narrow beaked jaws lined internally with flat, pavement-like crushing plates.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate turtle-like marine placodont with a flattened, armored body split into two shields, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Turtle-like marine placodont with a flattened, armored body split into two shields.
sources: [{"citation":"Rieppel, O. (2002). The skull of Psephoderma alpinum Meyer, 1858 (Reptilia: Placodontia). Fieldiana Geology.","url":"https://doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.5369"}]

name: Rhizodus
dietDetails: Apex predator of Carboniferous swamps, ambush hunting giant amphibians and early tetrapods.
discoveryHistory:
• First described by Richard Owen in 1840 from massive tooth specimens found near Edinburgh.
• Fossilized scales up to 30 cm across and 22 cm long tusk-teeth were recovered in Scottish coal fields.
• Biomechanical studies confirm massive pectoral fin musculature for rapid burst acceleration.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed enormous 22 cm (9 inch) tusk-like teeth anchored deeply into massive jaws.","Could likely lung onto land or shallow swamp margins to snatch terrestrial amphibians, similar to modern crocodiles.","Its skin was covered in heavy, overlapping cosmoid scales providing armor against rival aquatic predators.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate the largest known freshwater lobe-finned fish, reaching up to 7 meters in length, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: The largest known freshwater lobe-finned fish, reaching up to 7 meters in length.
sources: [{"citation":"Jeffery, J. E. (2001). Pectoral fin anatomy of Rhizodus hibberti (Rhizodontida, Sarcopterygii). Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1671/0272-4634(2001)021[0495:PFAORH]2.0.CO;2"}]

name: Gillicus
dietDetails: Filter-feeding teleost fish scooping up small fish and zooplankton in open sea waters.
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Western Interior Seaway","country":"United States","fossilFormation":"Smoky Hill Chalk"}
discoveryHistory:
• First named by Edward Drinker Cope in 1872.
• Famous for the 'Fish-Within-A-Fish' fossil at the Sternberg Museum where a 4.3m Xiphactinus contains an intact 2m Gillicus in its ribcage.
• Abundant in Kansas chalk deposits.
interestingFacts: ["Best known as the swallowed prey in the famous 14-foot Xiphactinus specimen at Hays, Kansas.","Possessed numerous fine, needle-like gill rakers used to strain small marine organisms from sea water.","Had deeply embedded, thin circular scales that reduced turbulence during swift schooling swims.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate slender, 2-meter long ichthyodectid fish with fine, toothless or tiny-toothed jaws, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Slender, 2-meter long ichthyodectid fish with fine, toothless or tiny-toothed jaws.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/42a51ccb-36af-4f42-9a74-548e42014dbc.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/42a51ccb-36af-4f42-9a74-548e42014dbc","license":"CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication","credit":"Jun-Hyeok Jang","taxon":"Ichthyodectidae (Representative: Jinjuichthys cheongi)","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Bardack, D. (1965). Anatomy and evolution of chirocentrid fishes. University of Kansas Paleontological Contributions.","url":"https://hdl.handle.net/1808/3814"}]

name: Yutyrannus huali
dietDetails: Apex predator of cool, temperate Early Cretaceous forests, hunting sauropods and iguanodontians.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by local fossil collectors in Liaoning Province, China, and acquired by Xu Xing.
• Formally described in Nature in April 2012 by Xu Xing and colleagues.
• Three nearly complete skeletons of varying ages preserved extensive filamentous plumage.
interestingFacts: ["Holds the record as the largest direct feather-bearing animal in Earth's history (9 meters long, 1.4 tonnes).","Feathers were 20 cm long filamentous proto-feathers providing insulation in Liaoning's chilly 10°C climate.","Possessed a high median crest along its snout used for species display and intra-species communication.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate largest known dinosaur with direct, fossilized evidence of feathers, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Largest known dinosaur with direct, fossilized evidence of feathers.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/5770eb59-b382-4867-bdcc-f304eb4f0020.png","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/5770eb59-b382-4867-bdcc-f304eb4f0020","license":"CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication","credit":"Tasman Dixon","taxon":"Yutyrannus huali","taxonMatch":"species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Xu, X. et al. (2012). A gigantic feathered dinosaur from the Lower Cretaceous of China. Nature.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10906"}]

name: Nanotyrannus lancensis
dietDetails: Fast, highly active predator hunting agile prey such as ornithomimids, pachycephalosaurs, and young dinosaurs.
discoveryHistory:
• Skull discovered in 1942 by Charles W. Gilmore and initially named Gorgosaurus lancensis.
• Renamed Nanotyrannus by Robert Bakker, Michael Williams, and Philip Currie in 1988.
• Long debated whether it is a valid distinct genus or a juvenile Tyrannosaurus rex; 2024 studies by Longrich & Saitta reignited support for its validity.
interestingFacts: ["Subject of one of the longest and most fiercely contested debates in paleontology history.","Had significantly more teeth (up to 36 in upper jaw) and larger forelimbs than adult T. rex.","Possessed extremely long, slender leg bones adapted for high-speed pursuit running.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate slender, long-limbed theropod measuring roughly 5 meters in length and weighing ~900 kg, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Slender, long-limbed theropod measuring roughly 5 meters in length and weighing ~900 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Longrich, N. R., & Saitta, E. T. (2024). Taxonomic Status of Nanotyrannus lancensis: A Distinct Genus of Small Tyrannosaurid. Fossil Studies.","url":"https://doi.org/10.3390/fossils2010003"}]

name: Palaeoloxodon antiquus
dietDetails: Mixed feeder browsing on broadleaf foliage, shrubs, and grasses in temperate European forests.
geographicRange: {"continent":"Europe, Asia","region":"Mediterranean & Central Europe","country":"Germany, United Kingdom, Italy, Greece","fossilFormation":"Ebbsfleet Valley deposits"}
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c0/Elephas_antiquus_Straight_tusked_elephant.jpg?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original","type":"art","credit":"Erwin S. Christman, published by H. Osborn, 'Men of the Old Stone Age' (Public domain)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AElephas%20antiquus%20Straight%20tusked%20elephant.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Formally described in 1847 by Hugh Falconer and Proby Cautley.
• Numerous butchered skeletons discovered across Europe alongside Neanderthal flint tools.
• Genomic analysis in 2017 revealed Palaeoloxodon is closely related to modern African forest elephants.
interestingFacts: ["One of the largest terrestrial mammals to ever walk the Earth, outsizing the Woolly Mammoth.","Possessed long, nearly straight tusks reaching up to 3.8 meters in length.","Coexisted with Neanderthals and early Homo sapiens, who actively hunted these leviathans with wooden spears.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate stood up to 4.2 meters tall at the shoulder and weighed up to 13-15 metric tonnes, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Stood up to 4.2 meters tall at the shoulder and weighed up to 13-15 metric tonnes.
sources: [{"citation":"Meyer, M. et al. (2017). Palaeogenomics of the straight-tusked elephant Palaeoloxodon antiquus. eLife.","url":"https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.25413"}]

name: Gryposuchus colombianus
dietDetails: Piscivorous specialist preying upon giant catfish, characins, and freshwater turtles in the Pebas Wetland.
geographicRange: {"continent":"South America","region":"Amazon & Orinoco Basins","country":"Colombia, Venezuela, Brazil","fossilFormation":"La Venta Formation, Urumaco Formation"}
discoveryHistory:
• First described by Langston in 1965 from fossils collected at La Venta, Colombia.
• Exceptionally complete skulls recovered from Miocene deposits in Venezuela and Peru.
• Represents one of the largest members of the gharial family Gavialidae.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed an extremely elongated, narrow snout packed with over 80 inter-locking needle teeth.","Inhabited the mega-wetlands of Miocene South America alongside giant caimans like Purussaurus.","The hook-like curvature at the tip of its snout helped hold onto slippery, armor-plated prehistoric catfish.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate giant gharial-like crocodilian reaching estimated lengths of 10 meters, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Giant gharial-like crocodilian reaching estimated lengths of 10 meters.
sources: [{"citation":"Riff, D. et al. (2010). Neogene giant South American crocodilians. Amazonia: Landscape and Species Evolution.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1002/9781444326680.ch15"}]

name: Plesiosuchus manselii
dietDetails: Apex marine predator hunting large prey including plesiosaurs, ichthyosaurs, and large fish.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/10/Geosaurini.png?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original","type":"art","credit":"Mark T. Young, Stephen L. Brusatte, Marco Brandalise de Andrade, Julia B. Desojo, Brian L. Beatty, Lorna Steel, Marta S. Fernández, Manabu Sakamoto, Jose Ignacio Ruiz-Omeñaca, Rainer R. Schoch. (CC BY 2.5)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AGeosaurini.png"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Named by Richard Owen in 1884 based on a skull found in Kimmeridge Bay, Dorset.
• Re-analyzed in 2012 by Mark Young and colleagues, establishing Plesiosuchus as the apex predator of Kimmeridgian seas.
interestingFacts: ["The largest metriorhynchid crocodilian ever discovered, outgrowing Geosaurus and Metriorhynchus.","Had wide-opening jaws with coarse serrations adapted for severing flesh from large marine vertebrates.","Shared marine habitats with Dakosaurus, dividing ecological niches based on skull mechanics.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate the largest known metriorhynchid marine crocodilian, reaching almost 7 meters, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: The largest known metriorhynchid marine crocodilian, reaching almost 7 meters.
sources: [{"citation":"Young, M. T. et al. (2012). The spatial and temporal range of Geosaurus and Plesiosuchus. PLoS ONE.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0044985"}]

name: Suchodus durobrivensis
dietDetails: Marine predator targeting hard-bodied marine prey and fast-swimming teleost fish.
geographicRange: {"continent":"Europe","region":"Oxford Clay Basin","country":"United Kingdom, France","fossilFormation":"Oxford Clay Formation"}
discoveryHistory:
• First described by Lydekker in 1890 from specimens collected near Peterborough, England.
• Re-erected as a distinct genus separate from Metriorhynchus by Young et al. in 2010.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed significantly shorter, stronger jaws than Metriorhynchus for crushing armored prey.","Equipped with paddle-shaped limbs and a tail fin for pelagic sea life.","Fossilized eye rings (sclerotic rings) show adaptations for deep diving.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate robust metriorhynchid crocodilian measuring 4.5 meters in length, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Robust metriorhynchid crocodilian measuring 4.5 meters in length.
sources: [{"citation":"Young, M. T. et al. (2010). Revision of the Metriorhynchinae (Crocodylomorpha: Thalattosuchia). Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1096-3642.2009.00600.x"}]

name: Edestus heinrichi
dietDetails: Marine predator using vertical scissor-like jaw whorls to slash soft-bodied prey and fish.
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America, Europe","region":"Illinois Basin","country":"United States, Russia","fossilFormation":"Carbondale Formation"}
discoveryHistory:
• First described by Joseph Leidy in 1855 from bracketed tooth whorls found in coal mines.
• 2019 jaw mechanics study confirmed vertical slashing jaw action.
interestingFacts: ["Did not shed worn teeth; new teeth grew in from the back, pushing old teeth forward into protruding curved brackets.","Jaws operated like a pair of hedge trimmers, thrashing up and down to slash prey.","Belonged to Eugeneodontida, closely related to modern chimaeras rather than true sharks.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate nicknamed the 'scissor-toothed shark'; reached lengths of up to 6 meters, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Nicknamed the 'Scissor-toothed Shark'; reached lengths of up to 6 meters.
sources: [{"citation":"Itano, W. M. (2019). Edestus, the scissor-toothed shark: jaw mechanics and predation. Mineralico.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1007/s12542-019-00448-9"}]

name: Pyroraptor olympius
dietDetails: Agile, feathered pack hunter preying upon dwarf titanosaurs and iguanodontians on European islands.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1992 following a forest fire at Mount Olympe near Trets, Provence, France.
• Formally described in 2000 by Ronan Allain and Philippe Taquet.
• Remains include distinctive sickle toe claws, teeth, limb bones, and vertebrae.
interestingFacts: ["Named 'Fire Thief' because its fossils were uncovered immediately after a major forest fire.","Possessed a curved 6.5 cm sickle claw on the second toe of each foot for gripping prey.","Fully covered in feathers with wing-like plumage along its forelimbs.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate small dromaeosaurid dinosaur measuring 1.6 meters long and standing knee-high, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Small dromaeosaurid dinosaur measuring 1.6 meters long and standing knee-high.
sources: [{"citation":"Allain, R., & Taquet, P. (2000). A new dromaeosaurid (Dinosauria, Theropoda) from the Upper Cretaceous of Haute-Provence. Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1016/S1251-8050(00)00212-0"}]

name: Dracovenator regenti
dietDetails: Predatory theropod hunting early sauropodomorphs like Massospondylus.
discoveryHistory:
• Holotype partial skull discovered on Upper Drakensberg farm in Eastern Cape, South Africa.
• Named in 2005 by Adam M. Yates.
• Close relative of the North American Dilophosaurus.
interestingFacts: ["One of the earliest apex theropod dinosaurs discovered in southern Africa.","Possessed paired bony crests running along the top of its skull.","Targeted abundant early sauropodomorph dinosaurs as primary prey.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate dilophosaurid theropod estimated at 5.5 to 6 meters long, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Dilophosaurid theropod estimated at 5.5 to 6 meters long.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/4bbb9887-c271-4f75-8246-dd78446e0f05.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/4bbb9887-c271-4f75-8246-dd78446e0f05","license":"Attribution 4.0 International","credit":"Cy Marchant","taxon":"Coelophysis arizonensis","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Yates, A. M. (2005). A new theropod dinosaur from the Early Jurassic of South Africa and its implications for the early evolution of Theropoda. Palaeontologia Africana.","url":"https://hdl.handle.net/10539/12711"}]

name: Sarcosaurus woodi
dietDetails: Early carnivorous theropod preying upon small reptiles and early herbivorous dinosaurs.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1913 near Barrow-upon-Soar, Leicestershire, by James W. Wood.
• Named by Charles William Andrews in 1921.
• Represents one of the oldest known Jurassic theropods in Europe.
interestingFacts: ["One of the earliest true Jurassic theropod dinosaurs discovered in the UK.","Possessed a small nasal horn or crest similar to Ceratosaurus.","Inhabited coastal mudflats alongside early marine reptiles.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate basal neotheropod measuring 3.5 meters in length, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Basal neotheropod measuring 3.5 meters in length.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/4d7d38eb-0973-4bac-b7c7-99e63c40fe82.png","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/4d7d38eb-0973-4bac-b7c7-99e63c40fe82","license":"CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication","credit":"Tasman Dixon","taxon":"Ceratosauridae (Representative: Ceratosaurus nasicornis)","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Ezcurra, M. D. et al. (2020). Enigmatic early theropod Sarcosaurus woodi re-evaluated. Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1093/zoolinnean/zlaa086"}]

name: Animantarx ramaljonesi
dietDetails: Low-level herbivore feeding on ferns, cycads, and low shrub vegetation.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1999 using radiological survey equipment by Ramal Jones.
• Formally described by Kenneth Carpenter, James Kirkland, Donald Burge, and John Bird in 1999.
• Discovered specifically due to radioactive signals emitted by fossilized bones.
interestingFacts: ["First dinosaur discovered exclusively via radiological radiation detection technology.","Possessed a heavily armored skull with small horn-like projections behind the eyes.","Lacked a tail club, relying instead on shoulder spikes and fused armor plates.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate small nodosaurid ankylosaur measuring approximately 3 meters, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Small nodosaurid ankylosaur measuring approximately 3 meters.
sources: [{"citation":"Carpenter, K. et al. (1999). A new nodosaurid (Dinosauria: Ankylosauria) from the Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah. Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1080/02724634.1999.10011140"}]

name: Segnosaurus galbinensis
dietDetails: Herbivorous theropod using long claws to hook branches and pluck leaves.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1973 in the Gobi Desert by Altangerel Perle.
• Formally described by Perle in 1979.
• Name-giver of the Segnosauria (now Therizinosauria) group.
interestingFacts: ["Bizarre theropod that evolved away from meat-eating to become a strict herbivore.","Possessed a massive pot belly to ferment tough plant vegetation.","Equipped with elongated, curved hand claws used to pull down tree branches.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate large therizinosaurid measuring 6 meters in length and weighing over 1 tonne, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Large therizinosaurid measuring 6 meters in length and weighing over 1 tonne.
sources: [{"citation":"Perle, A. (1979). Segnosauridae - a new family of theropods from the Late Cretaceous of Mongolia. Transactions of the Joint Soviet-Mongolian Paleontological Expedition.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/checkTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38712"}]

name: Bajadasaurus pronuspinax
dietDetails: Low-level browser feeding on ferns, horsetails, and low vegetation using forward spines as defense.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2013 in Neuquén Province, Patagonia, Argentina.
• Formally described in Scientific Reports in 2019 by Pablo Gallina and colleagues.
• Preserved skull, neck vertebrae, and spectacular elongated neural spines.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed extremely long, thin neural spines along its neck that curved forward over its head.","The neck spines were likely covered in keratin sheaths, acting as defensive spikes against predators while grazing.","Eyes were positioned high on its skull, allowing it to look out for predators while lowering its snout to eat.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate dicraeosaurid sauropod measuring 9 meters long with dramatic forward-pointing neck spines, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Dicraeosaurid sauropod measuring 9 meters long with dramatic forward-pointing neck spines.
sources: [{"citation":"Gallina, P. A. et al. (2019). A new long-spined dinosaur from Patagonia sheds light on sauropod defense mechanics. Scientific Reports.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-37943-3"}]

name: Fukuiraptor kitadaniensis
dietDetails: Medium-sized carnivore preying on ornithopods and sauropods in Early Cretaceous Japan.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1989 at the Kitadani Quarry in Katsuyama, Fukui Prefecture, Japan.
• Formally described in 2000 by Yoichi Azuma and Philip J. Currie.
• One of the most complete theropod skeletons found in Japan.
interestingFacts: ["Initially thought to be a dromaeosaurid due to a large hand claw, later recognized as a megaraptoran.","The state dinosaur mascot of Fukui Prefecture, Japan.","Possessed large hand claws used to grasp prey.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate medium-sized megaraptoran theropod reaching 4.2 meters in length, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Medium-sized megaraptoran theropod reaching 4.2 meters in length.
sources: [{"citation":"Azuma, Y., & Currie, P. J. (2000). A new carcharodontosaurid theropod from the Lower Cretaceous of Japan. Cretaceous Research.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1006/cres.2000.0223"}]

name: Fukuisaurus tetoriensis
dietDetails: Herbivorous iguanodontian browsing on horsetails, ferns, and early flowering plants.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1989 alongside Fukuiraptor in Katsuyama, Fukui, Japan.
• Described in 2003 by Yoichi Azuma and Pascal Godefroit.
• Preserved skull and jaw material showing unique kinetic chewing adaptations.
interestingFacts: ["Skull lacked the kinetic flexibility seen in advanced hadrosaurs, chewing with a rigid maxilla.","Coexisted with Fukuiraptor, Fukuititan, and Koshisaurus in Early Cretaceous Japan.","Equipped with a sharp beak for clipping tough vegetation.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate bipedal/quadrupedal iguanodontian measuring 4.7 meters long, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]

name: Leedsichthys problematicus
dietDetails: Giant filter-feeder straining zooplankton, small crustaceans, and jellyfish through gill basket mesh.
geographicRange: {"continent":"Europe, South America","region":"Tethys / Boreal Oceans","country":"United Kingdom, France, Germany, Chile","fossilFormation":"Oxford Clay Formation"}
discoveryHistory:
• First fragments collected in 1886 near Peterborough, England, by fossil collector Alfred Nicholson Leeds.
• Named 'problematicus' by Arthur Smith Woodward because giant fragmented bones were difficult to reconstruct.
• Comprehensive 2013 laser-scan study by Jeff Liston confirmed adult lengths between 16 and 16.5 meters.
interestingFacts: ["Holds the record as the largest bony fish in Earth's history, rivaling modern baleen whales in ecological role.","Possessed over 40,000 delicate mesh-like gill raker teeth to filter microscopic plankton.","Bite marks on Leedsichthys fins show it was hunted by giant marine predators like Liopleurodon and Metriorhynchus.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate the largest bony fish (osteichthyes) known to have ever existed, reaching 16.5 meters, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: The largest bony fish (Osteichthyes) known to have ever existed, reaching 16.5 meters.
sources: [{"citation":"Liston, J. J. et al. (2013). Growth, age and size of the giant Jurassic bony fish Leedsichthys problematicus. Mesozoic Fishes 5.","url":"https://www.researchgate.net/publication/258334460"}]

name: Suchomimus tenerensis
dietDetails: Semiaquatic predator snatching giant fish (Mawsonia) and young dinosaurs from Cretaceous rivers.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1997 in the Ténéré Desert of Niger by team led by Paul Sereno.
• Formally described in Science in November 1998.
• Skeleton roughly 70% complete including skull, arms, claws, and vertebrae.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed a narrow 1.2-meter long crocodile-like skull lined with 100 conical teeth.","Had a massive 30 cm sickle claw on its thumb used to spear fish.","Featured a low neural spine sail reaching up to 60 cm high along its back.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate large spinosaurid theropod measuring 11 meters in length and weighing nearly 4 tonnes, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Large spinosaurid theropod measuring 11 meters in length and weighing nearly 4 tonnes.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/2aa3ad0e-5026-436b-9998-f08d588d37c8.png","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/2aa3ad0e-5026-436b-9998-f08d588d37c8","license":"CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication","credit":"Jagged Fang Designs","taxon":"Suchomimus","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Sereno, P. C. et al. (1998). A long-snouted predatory dinosaur from Africa and the evolution of spinosaurids. Science.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1126/science.282.5392.1298"}]

name: Tropaeognathus mesembrinus
dietDetails: Ocean-going aerial piscivore skimming fish from the water surface using crested jaws.
discoveryHistory:
• Described in 1987 by Peter Wellnhofer from fossils in the Romualdo Formation, Brazil.
• 2013 skeleton specimen MN 6594-V described by Kellner et al. confirmed massive 8.2m wingspan.
interestingFacts: ["One of the largest pre-azhdarchid flying reptiles known, with an 8.2-meter wingspan.","Possessed large convex keel-like crests on the tips of both upper and lower jaws.","Crests acted as rudders to stabilize jaws while dipping into water at high speed to catch fish.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate giant anhanguerid pterosaur with a wingspan reaching 8.2 meters (27 feet), providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Giant anhanguerid pterosaur with a wingspan reaching 8.2 meters (27 feet).
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/27964a31-8e2c-4f92-9427-ec3608f3b645.png","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/27964a31-8e2c-4f92-9427-ec3608f3b645","license":"CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication","credit":"Dean Schnabel","taxon":"Criorhynchidae (Representative: Arthurdactylus conandoylei)","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Kellner, A. W. A. et al. (2013). The largest pterosaur from Gondwana and other new anhanguerids from Brazil. Anais da Academia Brasileira de Ciências.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1590/0001-37652013102912"}]

name: Coloborhynchus clavirostris
dietDetails: Coastal pelagic piscivore catching slippery marine fish with forward-pointing teeth.
discoveryHistory:
• Named by Richard Owen in 1874 based on a partial snout found in East Sussex, England.
• Re-evaluated by Rodrigues & Kellner in 2013, restricting the genus to European Valanginian strata.
interestingFacts: ["Featured a unique flattened front snout tip with teeth projecting forward at odd angles.","Equipped with a prominent crest along the front upper jaw.","Earliest recognized anhanguerid pterosaur in the European fossil record.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate pterosaur with an estimated wingspan of approximately 5 to 6 meters, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Pterosaur with an estimated wingspan of approximately 5 to 6 meters.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/27964a31-8e2c-4f92-9427-ec3608f3b645.png","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/27964a31-8e2c-4f92-9427-ec3608f3b645","license":"CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication","credit":"Dean Schnabel","taxon":"Ornithocheiridae (Representative: Arthurdactylus conandoylei)","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Rodrigues, T., & Kellner, A. W. A. (2013). Taxonomic review of the Ornithocheirus complex (Pterosauria). ZooKeys.","url":"https://doi.org/10.3897/zookeys.308.5559"}]

name: Arctodus simus
dietDetails: Hyper-carnivorous apex predator and giant kleptoparasite scavenging mammoth and bison kills.
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Great Plains & Coastlines","country":"United States, Canada, Mexico","fossilFormation":"Rancho La Brea tar pits, Riverbluff Cave"}
discoveryHistory:
• Formally described by Joseph Leidy in 1854.
• Abundant, exceptionally preserved bones recovered from the Rancho La Brea tar pits in California.
• Carbon isotope studies confirmed an overwhelmingly carnivorous diet.
interestingFacts: ["Stood over 3.4 meters (11 feet) tall on its hind legs, making it the largest terrestrial mammalian carnivore in North America.","Used its massive size to bully smaller predators like saber-toothed cats (Smilodon) away from fresh kills.","Possessed unusually long, slender legs allowing it to pace efficiently across vast distances.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate stood up to 1.8 meters tall at the shoulder and over 3.4 meters tall when standing on hind legs, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Stood up to 1.8 meters tall at the shoulder and over 3.4 meters tall when standing on hind legs.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/8d4b7834-9dd3-4f5a-84a7-99fa159a112a.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/8d4b7834-9dd3-4f5a-84a7-99fa159a112a","license":"CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication","credit":"Tracy Heath","taxon":"Arctodus simus","taxonMatch":"species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Matheus, P. E. (1995). Diet and ecology of polar bears and giant short-faced bears based on stable isotopes. Quaternary Research.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1006/qres.1995.1078"}]

name: Purussaurus brasiliensis
dietDetails: Apex apex predator eating giant rodents (Josephoartigasia), river turtles, sloths, and fish.
geographicRange: {"continent":"South America","region":"Amazon Basin","country":"Brazil, Peru, Venezuela","fossilFormation":"Solimões Formation, Urumaco Formation"}
discoveryHistory:
• First skull fragments discovered in 1892 along the Purus River by Barbosa Rodrigues.
• Formally reconstructed in 2015 by Tito Aureliano and colleagues, revealing incredible 69,000 N bite force.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed one of the strongest bite forces of any animal in Earth's history (~69,000 Newtons / 7 tonnes force).","Its massive skull measured 1.4 meters long and was immensely broad for crushing thick mammalian bones.","Consumed over 40 kilograms of meat per day to maintain its giant metabolic needs.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate giant caiman reaching 10.3 meters in length and weighing over 8.4 tonnes, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Giant caiman reaching 10.3 meters in length and weighing over 8.4 tonnes.
sources: [{"citation":"Aureliano, T. et al. (2015). Morphometry, Bite Force, and Paleobiology of the Late Miocene Caiman Purussaurus brasiliensis. PLoS ONE.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0117937"}]

name: Josephoartigasia monesi
nameMeaning: Named after José Gervasio Artigas and Álvaro Mones
dietDetails: Giant herbivore feeding on soft aquatic plants, grasses, and river vegetation.
geographicRange: {"continent":"South America","region":"Rio de la Plata Basin","country":"Uruguay","fossilFormation":"San José Formation"}
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/99/Josephoartigasia_monesi.jpg?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original","type":"art","credit":"Andrés Rinderknecht & Ernesto Blanco; Illustration: Gustavo Lecuona (CC BY-SA 2.5)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AJosephoartigasia%20monesi.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Complete 53 cm long fossil skull discovered in 1987 on the coast of San José, Uruguay.
• Formally described in 2008 by Andrés Rinderknecht and Ernesto Blanco in Proceedings of the Royal Society B.
interestingFacts: ["Holds the Guinness World Record as the largest rodent to ever exist on Earth.","Possessed enormous 30 cm incisors with a bite force equivalent to a tiger, used for digging or defense.","Replaced traditional ungulate herbivore niches in prehistoric South American river estuaries.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate the largest rodent ever discovered, weighing as much as a modern bull (~1,000 kg), providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: The largest rodent ever discovered, weighing as much as a modern bull (~1,000 kg).
sources: [{"citation":"Rinderknecht, A., & Blanco, R. E. (2008). The largest fossil rodent. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2007.1645"}]

name: Livyatan melvillei
nameMeaning: Leviathan named after Herman Melville (author of Moby-Dick)
dietDetails: Apex marine macroraptorial predator preying on medium-sized baleen whales, seals, and sharks.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2008 in the coastal desert of Pisco, Peru, by Klaas Post.
• Formally described in Nature in July 2010 by Olivier Lambert and team.
• Named in honor of Herman Melville, author of Moby-Dick.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed the largest functional biting teeth of any known animal in Earth's history (36 cm long and 12 cm wide).","Unlike modern sperm whales which feed on squid using toothless upper jaws, Livyatan had huge teeth in BOTH upper and lower jaws.","Coexisted and directly competed with Megalodon for marine mammalian prey in Miocene oceans.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate giant raptorial sperm whale measuring 13.5 to 17.5 meters and weighing up to 50 tonnes, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Giant raptorial sperm whale measuring 13.5 to 17.5 meters and weighing up to 50 tonnes.
sources: [{"citation":"Lambert, O. et al. (2010). The giant bite of a new raptorial sperm whale from the Miocene of Peru. Nature.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1038/nature09067"}]

name: Kelenken guillermoi
nameMeaning: Named after Kélenken (Patagonian demon spirit) and Guillermo Aguirre Zabala
dietDetails: Apex terrestrial predator using long legs to chase down prey and drive heavy hooked beak downwards.
discoveryHistory:
• Skull discovered in 1999 near Comallo village by high school student Guillermo Aguirre Zabala.
• Formally described in 2007 by Sara Bertelli, Luis M. Chiappe, and Claudia Tambussi.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed the largest head of any known bird in history, with a skull measuring 71.6 cm (28 inches) long.","Could sprint at estimated speeds exceeding 45 km/h to run down prehistoric mammals.","Killed prey by striking downwards with its massive eagle-like hooked beak like an axe.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate the largest terror bird known, standing over 3 meters tall with a 71 cm long head, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: The largest terror bird known, standing over 3 meters tall with a 71 cm long head.
sources: [{"citation":"Bertelli, S., Chiappe, L. M., & Tambussi, C. (2007). A new phorusrhacid (Aves: Cariamiformes) from the Middle Miocene of Patagonia. Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1671/0272-4634(2007)27[409:ANPACB]2.0.CO;2"}]

name: Varanus priscus
dietDetails: Apex predator ambush hunting giant marsupials (Diprotodon, Procoptodon) and giant birds.
discoveryHistory:
• Named Megalania prisca by Sir Richard Owen in 1859.
• Reclassified under the genus Varanus by Ralph Molnar in 2004.
• Coexisted with early Indigenous Australians prior to its extinction ~40,000 years ago.
interestingFacts: ["The largest terrestrial venomous squamate reptile in Earth's history.","Possessed venom glands in its lower jaws similar to its smaller living relative, the Komodo Dragon.","Serrated recumbent teeth allowed it to tear open heavy hide of giant extinct marsupials.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate the largest terrestrial lizard known to have ever lived, reaching up to 6 meters in length, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: The largest terrestrial lizard known to have ever lived, reaching up to 6 meters in length.
sources: [{"citation":"Fry, B. G. et al. (2009). A central role for venom in predation by Varanus komodoensis and Megalania. PNAS.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0810883106"}]

name: Daeodon shoshonensis
epoch: Late Oligocene to Early Miocene Epoch
dietDetails: Bone-crushing apex scavenger and opportunistic predator eating carcasses, roots, and small ungulates.
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Great Plains","country":"United States","fossilFormation":"Arikaree Group (Agate Fossil Beds)"}
discoveryHistory:
• Formally described in 1878 by Edward Drinker Cope.
• Famous 90 cm fossil skulls recovered from Agate Fossil Beds National Monument in Nebraska.
• Synonymized with Dinohyus hollandi by Peterson in 1909.
interestingFacts: ["Nicknamed the 'Hell Pig', though genetically closer to hippos and whales than true pigs.","Possessed a massive 90 cm (3 foot) skull with heavy bony cheek flanges (jugal flanges) for muscle attachment.","Heavily worn teeth show it routinely cracked open giant animal bones to extract nutrient-rich marrow.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate nicknamed 'hell pig'; stood 1.8 meters (6 feet) tall at the shoulder with a 90 cm skull, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Nicknamed 'Hell Pig'; stood 1.8 meters (6 feet) tall at the shoulder with a 90 cm skull.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/f9d16638-b5d8-4321-a0af-0cd67e4740be.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/f9d16638-b5d8-4321-a0af-0cd67e4740be","license":"CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication","credit":"Steven Traver","taxon":"Daeodon","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Effinger, J. A. (1998). Entelodontidae. Evolution of Tertiary Mammals of North America.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511542947.026"}]

name: Alioramus
dietDetails: Carnivorous predator preying on small-to-medium dinosaurs, oviraptorosaurs, and juvenile ornithischians.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by a Soviet-Mongolian paleontological expedition in the Gobi Desert in the early 1970s and formally described by Sergei Kurzanov in 1976.
interestingFacts: ["Distinguished by a prominent row of five bony crests or bumps along the bridge of its slender snout.","Possessed more teeth than any other tyrannosaurid (76 to 78 teeth), adapted for seizing smaller, agile prey.","Its slender proportions led researchers to suggest it occupied a distinct ecological niche compared to apex Tarbosaurus.","Histological analysis of Alioramus altai showed that even near-adult individuals maintained a long, gracile snout."]
sizeNotes: Based on subadult holotype PIN 3141/1, characterized by a slender gracile build and elongated skull.
sources: [{"citation":"Kurzanov, S. M. (1976). A new late Cretaceous carnosaur from Nogon-Tsav, Mongolia. Trudy Sovmestnaya Sovetsko-Mongol'skaya Paleontologicheskaya Ekspeditsiya.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38605"},{"citation":"Brusatte, S. L., Carr, T. D., Erickson, G. M., Bever, G. S., & Norell, M. A. (2009). A long-snouted, multi-horned tyrannosaurid from the Late Cretaceous of Mongolia. PNAS, 106(41), 17261-17266.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0906911106"}]

name: Saurornitholestes
dietDetails: Active carnivore preying on small mammals, lizards, frogs, and juvenile dinosaurs; also scavenged larger carcasses.
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Alberta / Montana","country":"Canada / United States","fossilFormation":"Dinosaur Park Formation"}
discoveryHistory: Discovered by Wann Langston Jr. in 1974 at Dinosaur Provincial Park, Alberta, and formally named by Hans-Dieter Sues in 1978.
interestingFacts: ["One of the most abundant small theropods discovered in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta.","A partial pterosaur bone (azhdarchid wing bone) was discovered with embedded Saurornitholestes teeth, indicating scavenging behavior.","Possessed specialized olfactory bulbs in the brain, suggesting a sharp sense of smell for tracking nocturnal prey.","Featured unusually large sickle claws relative to its body size compared to contemporary velociraptorines."]
sizeNotes: Lightly built dromaeosaurid with exceptionally long, slender hindlimbs and large sickle claws on the second toes.
sources: [{"citation":"Sues, H.-D. (1978). A new small theropod dinosaur from the Judith River Formation of Alberta, Canada. Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society, 62(4), 381-400.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1096-3642.1978.tb01043.x"},{"citation":"Currie, P. J., & Evans, D. C. (2019). Cranial anatomy of new specimens of Saurornitholestes langstoni and palaeoecology of Alberta dromaeosaurids. The Anatomical Record, 303(4), 690-715.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1002/ar.24241"}]

name: Deinocheirus
dietDetails: Bulk omnivore feeding on soft aquatic vegetation, water plants, freshwater fish, and small aquatic invertebrates.
discoveryHistory: First discovered in 1965 by Zofia Kielan-Jaworowska as giant mysterious arms; its bizarre complete body with duck-bill and dorsal sail was revealed in 2014 by Lee et al.
interestingFacts: ["Remained one of paleontology's greatest mysteries for nearly 50 years when only its gargantuan arms were known.","Featured a prominent sail-like hump along its back supported by tall neural spines and a fused pygostyle at the tail tip.","Fossilized stomach contents revealed fish scales alongside over 1,400 gastroliths used to grind tough plant matter.","Possessed a wide, toothless, duck-like bill ideal for scooping aquatic vegetation in Cretaceous wetlands."]
sizeNotes: The largest known ornithomimosaurian, sporting massive 2.4-meter arms ending in blunt, curved 20-centimeter claws.
sources: [{"citation":"Lee, Y. N., Barsbold, R., Currie, P. J., et al. (2014). Resolving the long-standing enigmas of a giant ornithomimosaur Deinocheirus mirificus. Nature, 515(7526), 257-260.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13874"}]

name: Erlikosaurus
dietDetails: Herbivore consuming foliage, ferns, fruits, and soft Cretaceous vegetation.
discoveryHistory: Found during a Soviet-Mongolian expedition in 1972 at Bayshin Tsav and formally named by Altangerel Perle in 1980.
interestingFacts: ["Provides the primary anatomical blueprint for the entire Therizinosauridae group thanks to its intact 25-centimeter skull.","Possessed a keratinous beak at the tip of its snout accompanied by small, leaf-shaped serrated teeth for stripping leaves.","Digital endocranial reconstructions revealed well-developed sense organs for hearing, balance, and spatial coordination.","Had slender, curved claws on its forelimbs used to hook high branches and pull foliage toward its mouth."]
sizeNotes: Known from the only exceptionally preserved complete skull of any therizinosaurid found to date (holotype MPC-D 100/111).
sources: [{"citation":"Perle, A. (1980). Segnosauria - a new infraorder of carnivorous dinosaurs. Trudy Sovmestnaya Sovetsko-Mongol'skaya Paleontologicheskaya Ekspeditsiya, 15, 87-103.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38634"},{"citation":"Lautenschlager, S., Rayfield, E. J., Altangerel, P., Zanno, L. E., & Witmer, L. M. (2012). The cranial paleoneurology of Erlikosaurus andrewsi. PLoS ONE, 7(12), e52289.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0052289"}]

name: Mastodonsaurus
dietDetails: Ambush predator hunting freshwater fish, temnospondyls, and small terrestrial archosaurs entering shallow waterways.
discoveryHistory: First described by Georg Friedrich von Jäger in 1828 based on a distinctive tooth cusp; complete massive skeletons were later uncovered in southern Germany.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed two enormous upward-pointing tusks on the lower jaw that poked completely through openings in the upper snout when the mouth closed.","Its reduced limbs and flattened aquatic body meant it lived almost entirely submerged in water.","Multiple fossil bonebeds show hundreds of individuals perished together in shrinking drought ponds during seasonal dry spells.","Lateral line sensory grooves along its skull allowed it to detect pressure waves generated by swimming prey."]
sizeNotes: One of the largest amphibians to ever exist, with a massive triangular skull reaching up to 1.4 meters in length.

name: Palaeoloxodon namadicus
nameMeaning: Ancient straight-tusked elephant of the Narmada
dietDetails: Megaherbivore grazing on grasses and browsing on trees, shrubs, and bamboo across Indian river valleys.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 1834 by Hugh Falconer and Proby Cautley in the Narmada Valley of Madhya Pradesh, India, and described in 1845.
interestingFacts: ["Considered by many paleontologists as the largest terrestrial mammal ever discovered, easily dwarfing modern elephants.","Characterized by a robust parietal-occipital cranial crest on its forehead that anchored massive neck muscles supporting its colossal head.","Coexisted with early hominins (such as archaic Homo / Narmada Man) throughout the Pleistocene of India.","Possessed nearly straight, massive upward-curving tusks that exceeded 3.5 meters in length."]
sizeNotes: Often cited as the largest land mammal of the Quaternary period, with shoulder heights reaching up to 4.5 meters and estimated weights up to 15-22 tonnes.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/e6beff81-167d-4882-b86f-24ef9a405835.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/e6beff81-167d-4882-b86f-24ef9a405835","license":"CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication","credit":"Steven Traver","taxon":"Palaeoloxodon","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}

Shoulder height, body mass, and shape of proboscideans. Acta Palaeontologica Polonica, 61(3), 537-574.","url":"https://doi.org/10.4202/app.00136.2014"}]

name: Tyrannotitan
dietDetails: Apex predator preying upon massive titanosaurian sauropods such as Patagotitan and Chubutisaurus.
discoveryHistory: Found on the 'La Juanita' farm in Chubut in 1999 and formally described by Fernando Novas and colleagues in 2005.
interestingFacts: ["One of the earliest known giant carcharodontosaurids, predating both Giganotosaurus and Mapusaurus.","Unlike its later relatives, its teeth were less blade-like and bore wrinkly, undulating enamel surfaces adapted for crushing flesh.","Possessed extraordinarily short and stout arms, showing early evolutionary reduction in forelimb size among giganotosaurines.","Lived alongside giant titanosaur sauropods, which it attacked using slashing, wound-inflicting bites."]
sizeNotes: Massive carcharodontosaurid comparable in size to Giganotosaurus and Carcharodontosaurus, with heavily built dorsal vertebrae.
sources: [{"citation":"Novas, F. E., de Valais, S., Vickers-Rich, P., & Rich, T. (2005). A large Cretaceous theropod from Patagonia, Argentina, and the evolution of carcharodontosaurids. Naturwissenschaften, 92(5), 226-230.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1007/s00114-005-0623-3"}]

name: Thalassodromeus
dietDetails: Terrestrial and aerial predator hunting small vertebrates, fish, squids, and lizards.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in calcium carbonate concretions in northeastern Brazil and described in 2002 by Alexander Kellner and Diogenes de Almeida Campos.
interestingFacts: ["Sported one of the largest cranial crests known relative to its skull, laced with extensive blood vessel impressions for thermoregulation and display.","Originally hypothesized to skim-feed, biomechanical studies later proved its neck and jaw could not withstand water resistance forces.","Operated as a terrestrial predator similar to modern storks, stalking small prey on the ground.","Its toothless, scissor-like jaws converged to a sharp tip capable of delivering powerful stabbing and slicing bites."]
sizeNotes: Wingspan of approximately 4.2 to 4.5 meters; skull length of 1.4 meters, with the cranial crest accounting for 75% of skull surface area.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/63ddffa8-a14d-46ca-a38f-548d3254df43.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/63ddffa8-a14d-46ca-a38f-548d3254df43","license":"CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication","credit":"Dean Schnabel","taxon":"Thalassodromeus sethi","taxonMatch":"species-specific"}

Science, 297(5580), 389-392.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1073186"},{"citation":"Humphries, S., Bonser, R. H., Witton, M. P., & Martill, D. M. (2007). Did pterosaurs skim hunt? Did any of them? PLoS Biology, 5(8), e204.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.0050204"}]

name: Infernodrakon
dietDetails: Carnivorous azhdarchoid stalking small dinosaurs, mammals, amphibians, and reptiles on Cretaceous floodplains.
discoveryHistory: Named and described based on holotype cervical and wing material recovered from the upper Hell Creek Formation of Montana.
interestingFacts: ["Coexisted directly with Tyrannosaurus rex, Triceratops, and the colossal giant pterosaur Quetzalcoatlus.","Demonstrates that medium-sized pterosaurs thrived alongside giant azhdarchids until the chicxulub asteroid impact.","Possessed elongated neck vertebrae and robust forelimbs adapted for efficient four-legged terrestrial stalking.","Features uniquely slender spear-like rostral morphology suggesting quick striking at small agile prey."]
sizeNotes: Mid-sized azhdarchid with an estimated wingspan of approximately 4.5 to 5.0 meters.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/6dd3a0b6-8c58-4205-9f10-45b6686c4cd0.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/6dd3a0b6-8c58-4205-9f10-45b6686c4cd0","license":"Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0)","credit":"jack liddle","taxon":"Azhdarcho lancicollis","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}

name: Zhuchengtyrannus
dietDetails: Apex predator preying upon giant hadrosaurids like Shantungosaurus and large ceratopsians like Sinoceratops.
discoveryHistory: Found in 2009 during quarry excavations in Zhucheng and named by David Hone and colleagues in 2011.
interestingFacts: ["Shares anatomical features with Tarbosaurus but differs in having a distinctive horizontal shelf on the maxilla.","Hunted the colossal hadrosaur Shantungosaurus, one of the largest non-sauropod dinosaurs to ever walk the Earth.","Lived in a floodplain ecosystem characterized by catastrophic mass mortality events that preserved thousands of dinosaur bones.","Bore massive, bone-crushing jaws with deep rooted teeth designed to withstand extreme lateral biting forces."]
sizeNotes: One of the largest known tyrannosaurids, nearly matching Tyrannosaurus rex and Tarbosaurus in maxilla and dentary dimensions.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/f05e56c4-83bc-4809-8c2e-fd30c0b0bba2.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/f05e56c4-83bc-4809-8c2e-fd30c0b0bba2","license":"Attribution 3.0 Unported (CC BY 3.0)","credit":"Conty (vectorized by T. Michael Keesey)","taxon":"Tyrannosaurus magnus","taxonMatch":"species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Hone, D. W. E., Wang, K., Sullivan, C., et al. (2011). A new, large tyrannosaurine theropod from the Upper Cretaceous of China. Cretaceous Research, 32(4), 495-503.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cretres.2011.03.005"}]

name: Quinkana
dietDetails: Apex terrestrial predator hunting giant marsupials like Diprotodon, giant kangaroos (Procoptodon), and flightless birds.
discoveryHistory: First described by Ralph Molnar in 1981 from Pliocene-Pleistocene cave and river deposits in northern Queensland.
interestingFacts: ["Unlike modern semi-aquatic crocodiles, Quinkana was fully terrestrial with upright legs capable of galloping pursuit.","Equipped with ziphodont teeth (laterally flattened and serrated like steak knives) designed for slicing mammal flesh.","One of Australia's apex predators alongside the giant monitor lizard Megalania and marsupial lion Thylacoleo.","Surviving until around 40,000 years ago, it encountered early indigenous Australians arriving on the continent."]
sizeNotes: Ziphodont terrestrial crocodile with laterally compressed, recurved serrated teeth and an erect walking posture.
sources: [{"citation":"Molnar, R. E. (1981). Pleistocene ziphodont crocodilians of Queensland. Records of the Australian Museum, 33(19), 803-834.","url":"https://doi.org/10.3853/j.0067-1975.33.1981.198"}]

name: Haast's Eagle
dietDetails: Apex avian predator specialized in taking down giant flightless moa up to 15 times its own weight.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 1871 by F. Fuller at Glenmark and described by Julius von Haast as Harpagornis moorei (later reclassified into Hieraaetus by Bunce et al. 2005).
interestingFacts: ["Struck its prey with force equivalent to a concrete block falling from an eight-story building, crushing the pelvis of giant moa.","Possessed relatively short wings for its massive weight, adapted for maneuvering through dense southern beech forests.","Ancient Māori oral tradition remembers the eagle as the 'Pouākai', a terrifying man-eating raptor from the high mountains.","DNA analysis revealed its closest living relative is the tiny Little Eagle, demonstrating rapid evolutionary island gigantism."]
sizeNotes: Wingspan estimated at 2.6 to 3.0 meters; the largest eagle known to have existed, with talons matching those of a tiger.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/ca85a325-a3e4-4d65-ba6f-77be07f3fd4b.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/ca85a325-a3e4-4d65-ba6f-77be07f3fd4b","license":"CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication","credit":"Rohit N","taxon":"Hieraaetus pennatus","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Bunce, M., et al. (2005). Extreme reversed sexual size dimorphism in the extinct New Zealand eagle. PLoS Biology, 3(1), e9.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.0030009"}]

name: Zhejiangopterus
dietDetails: Terrestrial stalker feeding on small vertebrates, lizards, eggs, and invertebrates.
discoveryHistory: Found in 1986 in Linhai County by a local quarry worker and described in 1994 by Cai Zhengquan and Wei Feng.
interestingFacts: ["One of the most anatomically complete azhdarchid pterosaurs ever discovered, providing critical data on azhdarchid neck structure.","Lacked the exaggerated cranial crests seen in many other pterosaurs, featuring a low, elongate, crestless skull with a sharp beak.","Its long neck vertebrae lacked cervical ribs, making the neck stiff and held upright like a modern stork.","Biomechanical analysis indicates it spent extensive time walking quadrupedally on land, picking off prey in open woodlands."]
sizeNotes: Wingspan of approximately 3.5 meters; known from multiple well-preserved complete skeletons including juvenile and adult specimens.
sources: [{"citation":"Cai, Z., & Wei, F. (1994). On a new pterosaur (Zhejiangopterus linhaiensis gen. et sp. nov.) from Upper Cretaceous in Linhai, Zhejiang, China. Vertebrata PalAsiatica, 32(3), 181-194.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=64319"}]

name: Glyptodon
dietDetails: Low-browsing herbivore and grazer feeding on coarse grasses, roots, and riparian vegetation.
geographicRange: {"continent":"South America","region":"Pampas & Gran Chaco","country":"Argentina / Brazil / Uruguay","fossilFormation":"Luján Formation"}
discoveryHistory: First described by Sir Richard Owen in 1839 based on fossils collected in South America during Charles Darwin's voyage on HMS Beagle.
interestingFacts: ["Its rigid carapace was so strong and spacious that early indigenous humans in South America used empty shells as shelters.","The tail was encased in a series of flexible bony rings ending in a blunt sheath used for defense against predators like Smilodon.","Fused cervical and thoracic vertebrae formed a solid bony bridge to support the tremendous weight of its armor dome.","Survived until approximately 10,000 years ago, where hunting by early human populations contributed to its extinction."]
sizeNotes: Massive armadillo relative with a domed protective shell composed of more than 1,000 fused osteoderms.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/936735ed-c08a-4315-b291-1a19ca4e4ffd.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/936735ed-c08a-4315-b291-1a19ca4e4ffd","license":"CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication","credit":"Celeste Luna","taxon":"Glyptodon","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Owen, R. (1839). Description of a tooth and part of the skeleton of the Glyptodon clavipes. Transactions of the Geological Society of London, 6, 81-106.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1144/transgslb.6.1.81"}]

name: Thanatotheristes
nameMeaning: Reaper of death, honoring De Groots
dietDetails: Apex predator preying upon early ceratopsians like Xenoceratops and hadrosauroids.
discoveryHistory: Found along the Bow River in Alberta in 2010 by local hikers John and Sandra De Groot, and described in 2020 by Jared Voris and colleagues.
interestingFacts: ["Nicknamed the 'Reaper of Death', it is the oldest named tyrannosaurid discovered in Canada, predating T. rex by about 12 million years.","Distinguished by a unique series of vertical ridges along the upper jaw margin (maxilla) in front of the eye socket.","Forms a distinct clade (Daspletosaurini) with Daspletosaurus, demonstrating that tyrannosaurids were ecologically partitioned into distinct lineages.","Deep, robust jaw construction indicates it delivered crushing bites to disable thick-skinned ceratopsian prey."]
sizeNotes: Oldest known tyrannosaurid from northern North America, with an adult skull measuring approximately 80 cm.
sources: [{"citation":"Voris, J. T., Therrien, F., Zelenitsky, D. K., & Brown, C. M. (2020). A new tyrannosaurine from the Canadian Late Cretaceous Foremost Formation. Cretaceous Research, 110, 104388.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cretres.2020.104388"}]

name: Gigantspinosaurus
dietDetails: Low-browsing herbivore feeding on cycads, bennettitaleans, ferns, and horsetails in Jurassic river basins.
discoveryHistory: Uncovered in 1985 in Zigong, Sichuan, and formally described in 1992 by Ouyang Hui.
interestingFacts: ["Sported the largest shoulder spines (parascapular spines) of any known stegosaur, flaring backward over a meter in length.","In contrast to its giant shoulder spines, the paired plates running down its neck and back were remarkably small and rounded.","Considered a basal member of Stegosauria, preserving primitive traits transitional between early armored dinosaurs and derived stegosaurids.","Skin impressions discovered with the specimen revealed small, rounded, non-overlapping polygonal scales covering the body."]
sizeNotes: Basal stegosaurian famous for its gargantuan shoulder spines, which were at least twice the length of its shoulder blades.
sources: [{"citation":"Ouyang, H. (1992). Discovery of Gigantspinosaurus sichuanensis and its scapular spine. Abstracts of the 5th Symposium of the Chinese Society of Vertebrate Paleontology, 47-49.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=66516"}]

name: Gigantoraptor
dietDetails: Omnivore or herbivore consuming high foliage, seeds, tubers, and opportunistically small vertebrates with its robust beak.
discoveryHistory: Accidentally unearthed in 2005 in front of a film crew filming a Japanese documentary on sauropod fossils; named in 2007 by Xu Xing et al.
interestingFacts: ["Reached a colossal size comparable to tyrannosaurids while retaining the light, bird-like skeletal features and toothless beak of oviraptorosaurs.","Bone histology of the holotype (LH V0011) revealed it was an 11-year-old subadult that was still actively growing at the time of death.","Despite weighing two tonnes, it had proportionally long, slender hind legs, indicating it was one of the fastest runners of its size.","Preserved pennaceous feathers on related oviraptorosaurs confirm that Gigantoraptor possessed feathered forelimbs used for brooding or display."]
sizeNotes: By far the largest known oviraptorosaurian, growing nearly 35 times heavier than most other oviraptorosaurs.
sources: [{"citation":"Xu, X., Tan, Q., Wang, J., Zhao, X., & Tan, L. (2007). A gigantic bird-like dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of China. Nature, 447(7146), 841-844.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1038/nature05849"}]

name: Rinchenia
dietDetails: Omnivore feeding on seeds, nuts, foliage, eggs, mollusks, and small vertebrates in Cretaceous river floodplains.
discoveryHistory: Found in 1984 in the Nemegt Basin; originally described by Rinchen Barsbold as Oviraptor mongoliensis, and placed in its own genus Rinchenia in 1997 by Halszka Osmólska.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed a dramatically tall, bulbous casque-like skull crest made of delicate porous bone, resembling that of a modern cassowary.","The crest served primarily as a visual display structure for species recognition and sexual selection in the lush Nemegt environment.","Equipped with an exceptionally robust, short lower jaw and toothless keratinous beak capable of cracking hard plant seeds and shellfish.","Its fused tail vertebrae (pygostyle) supported a fan of plumage used in mating displays."]
sizeNotes: Known from holotype MPC-D 100/32A, featuring a remarkably tall, thin, dome-like cranial crest.

name: Coelurosauravus
nameMeaning: Grandfather of hollow lizards of Eliva
dietDetails: Insectivore hunting arboreal insects, early cockroaches, and arthropods within Permian conifer canopies.
discoveryHistory: First described by French paleontologist Jean Piveteau in 1926 based on a fossil discovered in Madagascar.
interestingFacts: ["The earliest known gliding vertebrate in the fossil record, predating gliding dinosaurs and pterosaurs by tens of millions of years.","Unlike modern flying lizards whose wings are supported by ribs, Coelurosauravus sprouted specialized bony rods completely separate from the rib cage.","Possessed a heavily serrated parietal crest on the back of its skull adorned with pointed spines, resembling modern horned chameleons.","Equipped with curved, sharp claws well suited for gripping and scrambling vertically along ancient tree bark."]
sizeNotes: Slender gliding diapsid reptile with a body length of around 40 cm and a delicate wing membrane.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/04de6188-2504-45c6-9cf0-a804845f8c18.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/04de6188-2504-45c6-9cf0-a804845f8c18","license":"Attribution 3.0 Unported (CC BY 3.0)","credit":"Scott Reid","taxon":"Weigeltisaurus jaekeli","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
