Gliding mechanism in the Late Permian reptile Coelurosauravus. Science, 275(5305), 1450-1452.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1126/science.275.5305.1450"}]

name: Linhenykus
dietDetails: Specialized insectivore using its single stout thumb claw to dig into subterranean ant and termite mounds.
discoveryHistory: Found in 2008 in red sandstone beds at Bayan Mandahu by Jonah Choiniere and Michael Pittman, and described in 2011 by Xu Xing et al.
interestingFacts: ["The only known non-avian dinosaur to possess just a single functional finger (a stout clawed thumb) on each forelimb.","The second and third fingers were entirely absent or reduced to vestigial specks of bone, representing the extreme endpoint of theropod arm reduction.","Like modern pangolins and anteaters, its hyper-specialized single claws were adapted for ripping into hardened insect nests.","Had long, gracile bird-like hind legs capable of rapid running across arid desert dunes."]
sizeNotes: Tiny alvarezsaurid weighing under half a kilogram, famous for having only one functional digit on each hand.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/a724b06d-541b-42ac-8cea-b84f985653c6.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/a724b06d-541b-42ac-8cea-b84f985653c6","license":"Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0)","credit":"Jaime Headden","taxon":"Alvarezsaurus calvoi","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Xu, X., Sullivan, C., Pittman, M., et al. (2011). A monodactyl nonavian dinosaur and the complex evolution of the alvarezsauroid hand. PNAS, 108(6), 2338-2342.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1011052108"}]

name: Stomatosuchus
dietDetails: Piscivore and filter feeder straining small fish, crustaceans, and plankton using an expandable pelican-like throat pouch.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 1911 by Ernst Stromer in the Bahariya Oasis, Egypt, and described in 1925; tragically, the sole holotype skull was destroyed during an Allied bombing raid on Munich in 1944.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed an entirely toothless lower jaw paired with only tiny conical teeth in the upper jaw, unique among giant crocodylomorphs.","Believed to have possessed a massive, flexible gular throat pouch like a pelican to trap shoals of freshwater fish.","The only known fossil specimen was destroyed when the Alte Akademie museum in Munich was bombed during World War II.","Coexisted in North Africa's mangrove swamps with Spinosaurus and Carcharodontosaurus."]
sizeNotes: Giant crocodile with a flattened, shovel-shaped skull nearly 2 meters long, featuring a completely toothless lower jaw.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/f7d45c6d-e506-4826-8ffe-3f75d588d378.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/f7d45c6d-e506-4826-8ffe-3f75d588d378","license":"Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 Unported (CC BY-SA 3.0)","credit":"Stanton F. Fink, vectorized by Zimices","taxon":"Stomatosuchus inermis","taxonMatch":"species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Stromer, E. (1925). Ergebnisse der Forschungsreisen Prof. E. Stromers in den Wüsten Ägyptens. 7. Stomatosuchus inermis Stromer. Abhandlungen der Bayerischen Akademie der Wissenschaften.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38458"}]

name: Kariridraco
dietDetails: Frugivore and opportunistic omnivore feeding on gymnosperm fruits, seeds, and small vertebrates in coastal forests.
discoveryHistory: Named and described in 2021 by Gabriela Cerqueira and colleagues from a well-preserved skull excavated in northeastern Brazil.
interestingFacts: ["Distinguished by a sharp, deep sagittal cranial crest that curved downward along the premaxilla at a unique 45-degree angle.","Features unusually deep premaxillary margins and short, toothless, downturned jaws specialized for harvesting hard prehistoric fruits.","Named in honor of both the indigenous Kariri ethnic nation and the comic book heroine Diana Prince (Wonder Woman).","Belongs to the Tapejarinae, an endemic clade of ornate-crested pterosaurs that diversified rapidly across Gondwana."]
sizeNotes: Tapejarid pterosaur with a well-preserved skull and jaws exhibiting an estimated wingspan of approximately 2.5 meters.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/f075aa92-c901-400d-89c2-c2a9087c51da.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/f075aa92-c901-400d-89c2-c2a9087c51da","license":"Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0)","credit":"Cy Marchant","taxon":"Europejara olcadesorum","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Cerqueira, G. M., Santos, M. A., Marks, M. F., Sayão, J. M., & Pinheiro, F. L. (2021). A new tapejarine pterosaur from the Upper Cretaceous of Brazil. Historical Biology, 34(5), 875-885.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1080/08912963.2021.1955844"}]

name: Megabalaena
dietDetails: Bulk filter-feeder swallowing dense swarms of euphausiids (krill), copepods, and small schooling fish.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/68/Megabalaena_%28life_restoration%29.png","type":"art","credit":"Y. Tanaka, T. Kimura, T. Shinmura, H. Ohira & H. Furusawa (CC BY 4.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Megabalaena_(life_restoration).png"}]
discoveryHistory: Found in 2004 along the riverbed of the Aoki River in Nagano, Japan, and described in 2024 by Yoshihiro Tanaka and colleagues.
interestingFacts: ["Represents one of the earliest occurrences of gigantism among true right whales, demonstrating gigantism evolved earlier than previously thought.","Possessed a strongly arched rostrum and deep lower jaw specifically adapted to house very long baleen plates.","Unlike most modern right whales restricted to cold polar seas, Megabalaena inhabited warm temperate coastal waters in the Miocene Pacific.","Well-preserved auditory bulla and skull bones provide crucial evolutionary clues linking archaic cetotheres to living right whales."]
sizeNotes: Early giant true right whale (Balaenidae) reaching lengths comparable to modern northern right whales.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/a16c832f-cace-4c9e-af46-939cad395c3a.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/a16c832f-cace-4c9e-af46-939cad395c3a","license":"Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0)","credit":"Cy Marchant","taxon":"Megabalaena sapporoensis","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
closestLivingRelatives: ["North Atlantic Right Whale (Eubalaena glacialis)","Bowhead Whale (Balaena mysticetus)"]
sources: [{"citation":"Tanaka, Y., Kimura, T., Shinmura, T., Ohira, H., & Furusawa, H. (2024). A new late Miocene right whale (Balaenidae) from Japan and the evolution of body size in baleen whales. Journal of Systematic Palaeontology, 22(1), 2321453.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1080/14772019.2024.2321453"}]

name: Scylacosaurus
dietDetails: Active carnivorous predator preying on small dicynodonts, parareptiles, and early archosauromorphs.
discoveryHistory: First described by famed South African paleontologist Robert Broom in 1903 from Karoo Basin deposits near Colesberg.
interestingFacts: ["Equipped with prominent mammalian-style canine fangs and sharp postcanine teeth, reflecting the transition toward mammal-like carnivory.","Possessed deep grooves on its maxillary bones that some researchers hypothesize may have housed early venom delivery glands.","Endocranial casts indicate it had an acute sense of smell and whisker pits on the snout indicating tactile facial hair.","Thrived across southern Gondwana shortly before the devastating Permian-Triassic extinction event."]
sizeNotes: Medium-sized basal therocephalian with a long, slender snout and prominent canine tusks.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/6ecdac12-8832-401b-b6e2-8474dbc41b6a.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/6ecdac12-8832-401b-b6e2-8474dbc41b6a","license":"Public Domain Mark 1.0","credit":"Dmitry Bogdanov (vectorized by T. Michael Keesey)","taxon":"Scylacosaurus","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}

name: Apolithabatis
dietDetails: Benthic feeder preying on crustaceans, mollusks, bivalves, and small reef fish in shallow Tethys lagoons.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b0/Apolithabatis_%28life_restoration%29.png","type":"art","credit":"J. Türtscher, P. L. Jambura, F. Spindler & J. Kriwet (CC BY 4.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Apolithabatis_(life_restoration).png"}]
discoveryHistory: Named and described in 2024 by Julia Türtscher and an international team of paleoichthyologists from exceptionally preserved Monte Bolca fossils.
interestingFacts: ["Preserved in the world-famous Monte Bolca Lagerstätte with complete mineralized cartilage, tooth pavement plates, and skin outlines intact.","Equipped with flattened crushing dental plates arranged in pavement patterns, designed to crush thick-shelled crabs and gastropods.","Inhabited the tropical coral reef atolls of the western Tethys Ocean during the early Eocene thermal optimum.","Demonstrates that modern eagle ray swimming dynamics and reef foraging adaptations were already fully established 50 million years ago."]
sizeNotes: Disc width of approximately 75 cm with an elongated whip-like tail bearing a serrated defensive spine.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/ebdc09b9-659e-40e7-9323-1ac53d650aa3.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/ebdc09b9-659e-40e7-9323-1ac53d650aa3","license":"CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication","credit":"M Kolmann","taxon":"Aetobatus","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Türtscher, J., Jambura, P. L., Spindler, F., & Kriwet, J. (2024). Morphological and phylogenetic revision of batoid fishes from the Eocene of Monte Bolca, Italy. Journal of Paleontology.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1017/jpa.2024.12"}]

name: Jormungandr
dietDetails: Apex marine predator preying on cephalopods, hesperornithiform diving birds, sea turtles, and bony fish.
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Pembina Gorge, North Dakota","country":"United States","fossilFormation":"Pierre Shale Formation"}
discoveryHistory: Found in 2015 along the Pembina River in Cavalier County, North Dakota, and described in 2023 by Amelia Zietlow, Clint Boyd, and Mark Norell.
interestingFacts: ["Represents a crucial 'missing link' mosasaur documenting how plioplatecarpines transitioned into apex giants like Mosasaurus.","Retained primitive characteristics including 11 ribs above the pelvis while evolving advanced, crushing jaw morphology.","Inhabited the frigid, nutrient-rich waters of the Western Interior Seaway which split North America in half.","Its fossil skull preserves distinct rugose brow ridges above the eye sockets that may have supported protective structures."]
sizeNotes: Transitional mosasaur exhibiting an intermediate mosaic of primitive Clidastes-like and advanced Mosasaurus-like cranial traits.
sources: [{"citation":"Zietlow, A. R., Boyd, C. A., & Norell, M. A. (2023). Jormungandr walhallaensis, a new mosasaurine from the Late Cretaceous of North Dakota. Bulletin of the American Museum of Natural History, 464, 1-108.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1206/0003-0090.464.1.1"}]

name: Plotosaurus
dietDetails: High-speed pursuit predator hunting fast-swimming pelagic fish, belemnites, and ammonites in the open Pacific Ocean.
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Fresno County & San Joaquin Valley, California","country":"United States","fossilFormation":"Moreno Formation"}
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 1937 by high school student Allan Bennison in the Panoche Hills of California, and named by Charles Lewis Camp in 1942.
interestingFacts: ["The pinnacle of mosasaur hydrodynamic evolution: possessed a stiff, streamlined fusiform body resembling an ichthyosaur or tuna.","Unlike serpentine mosasaurs that undulated their entire bodies, Plotosaurus swam using carangiform locomotion powered strictly by a crescent-shaped tail fin.","Skin impressions revealed tiny, tightly packed keeled scales that significantly reduced water friction during high-speed chases.","Large eyes equipped with sclerotic rings allowed it to hunt in deep, dimly lit offshore Pacific waters."]
sizeNotes: The most hydrodynamically advanced mosasaur known, sporting narrow, streamlined flippers and a stiffened, carangiform torso.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/5d6d9f55-3d55-4f9b-ad95-e07bad213d1e.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/5d6d9f55-3d55-4f9b-ad95-e07bad213d1e","license":"Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 Unported (CC BY-SA 3.0)","credit":"Dmitry Bogdanov (original drawing)","taxon":"Halisaurus arambourgi","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Camp, C. L. (1942). California Mosasaurs. Memoirs of the University of California, 13, 1-68.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=36407"},{"citation":"Lindgren, J., Jagt, J. W., & Caldwell, M. W. (2007). A fishy mosasaur: the axial skeleton of Plotosaurus and its bearing on locomotion in derived mosasaurs. Palaeontology, 50(6), 1399-1414.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1475-4983.2007.00720.x"}]

name: Thanatosdrakon
nameMeaning: Dragon of death, winged serpent deity
dietDetails: Apex carnivorous predator preying on small-to-medium terrestrial vertebrates, dinosaur hatchlings, and reptiles.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Mendoza Province, Argentina during civil works construction and described in 2022 by Leonardo D. Ortiz David, Bernardo J. González Riga, and Alexander W. A. Kellner based on holotype UNCUYO-LD 307 and a gigantic paratype UNCUYO-LD 350.
interestingFacts: ["The largest pterosaur ever discovered in South America, possessing an immense estimated wingspan of approximately 9 meters (30 feet).","One of the oldest known giant azhdarchids, living millions of years before the famous terminal Cretaceous giants Quetzalcoatlus and Hatzegopteryx.","Its generic name translates to \"dragon of death\" (Thanatos + drakon), while the species epithet honors Amaru, the mythical winged flying serpent in Quechua Andean cosmology.","Skeletal adaptations in its cervical vertebrae and robust limb girdles indicate it was a terrestrial stalker that hunted prey efficiently on the ground in semi-arid braided floodplains."]
sizeNotes: Based on holotype UNCUYO-LD 307 (~7 m wingspan) and large adult paratype UNCUYO-LD 350 (~9 m wingspan).
sources: [{"citation":"Ortiz David, L. D., González Riga, B. J., & Kellner, A. W. A. (2022). Thanatosdrakon amaru, gen. et sp. nov., an azhdarchid pterosaur from the upper Cretaceous of Mendoza, Argentina. Cretaceous Research, 135, 105180.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cretres.2022.105180"}]

name: Oxalaia
dietDetails: Piscivore and opportunistic carnivore hunting giant lobe-finned coelacanths (Mawsonia), sawfish, and coastal terrestrial fauna.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 1999 on Cajual Island, Maranhão, Brazil, and described in 2011 by Alexander W. A. Kellner and colleagues based on holotype MN 6117-V. Tragic loss occurred in September 2018 when the holotype was destroyed in the National Museum of Brazil fire.
interestingFacts: ["The largest carnivorous dinosaur discovered in Brazil, estimated between 12 and 14 meters (39 to 46 feet) in total length and weighing 5 to 7 tonnes.","A true spinosaurine theropod closely related to the African Spinosaurus aegyptianus, demonstrating a paleobiogeographic connection between South America and Africa during the mid-Cretaceous.","Its generic name honors Oxalá, the supreme male deity in Afro-Brazilian Candomblé religion, while quilombensis recognizes the quilombos of Cajual Island established by escaped African slaves.","Possessed a distinctly expanded spoon-shaped terminal rosette at the tip of its long snout housing paired premaxillary teeth adapted to snatching slippery aquatic prey."]
sizeNotes: Based on holotype premaxillae MN 6117-V and isolated maxilla fragment MN 6119-V, scaled against Spinosaurus.
sources: [{"citation":"Kellner, A. W. A., Machado, E. B., Azevedo, S. A. K., Henriques, D. D. R., & Carvalho, L. B. (2011). A new dinosaur (Theropoda, Spinosauridae) from the Cretaceous (Cenomanian)-Alcântara Formation, Cajual Island, Brazil. Anais da Academia Brasileira de Ciências, 83(1), 99-108.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1590/S0001-37652011000100006"}]

name: Clidastes
dietDetails: Agile marine predator preying on cephalopods, teleost fish, marine birds (such as Ichthyornis), and smaller marine reptiles.
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Western Interior Seaway & Gulf Coast","country":"United States","fossilFormation":"Niobrara Formation & Mooreville Chalk"}
discoveryHistory: Named in 1868 by pioneering American paleontologist Edward Drinker Cope based on an articulated skeleton from Uniontown, Alabama. Cope was amazed by its interlocking vertebral articulations.
interestingFacts: ["One of the fastest and most agile of all mosasaurs, measuring between 3 and 5.5 meters (10 to 18 feet) with a slender, hydrodynamically streamlined body.","Its generic name refers to its unique interlocking \"key\" joints (zygosphene-zygantrum articulations) that stabilized its spinal column during rapid lateral undulations.","Possessed a downward-bent caudal fluke supporting a crescent-shaped shark-like vertical tail fin that produced rapid bursts of forward acceleration.","Coprolites and tooth marks confirm it regularly hunted diving marine avians such as Ichthyornis and Hesperornis in coastal inland seas."]
sizeNotes: Based on complete articulated skeletons from the Mooreville Chalk and Smoky Hill Chalk.
sources: [{"citation":"Cope, E. D. (1868). Remarks on a new enaliosaurian, Elasmosaurus platyurus, and Clidastes propython. Proceedings of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia, 20, 92-93.","url":"https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/26298918"},{"citation":"Lindgren, J., Polcyn, M. J., & Young, B. A. (2011). Skin pigmentation provides evidence of convergent melanism in extinct marine reptiles. Nature, 506(7489), 484-488.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12899"}]

name: Protoceratops
dietDetails: Herbivorous low-level browser equipped with a sharp shearing keratinous beak adapted to clipping tough desert vegetation, scrub roots, and cycads.
discoveryHistory: Found in 1922 during the Central Asiatic Expeditions led by Roy Chapman Andrews at the Flaming Cliffs (Bayn Dzak), Gobi Desert. Described in 1923 by Walter Granger and William King Gregory.
interestingFacts: ["Famed worldwide for the iconic \"Fighting Dinosaurs\" specimen discovered in 1971, preserved locked in mortal combat with a Velociraptor that was buried instantly by a collapsing sand dune.","Unlike its massive ceratopsid descendants (like Triceratops), Protoceratops lacked large brow horns, relying on a robust bony neck frill and muscular jaw adductors.","Hundreds of complete skeletons representing every ontogenetic stage—from embryos in nests and hatchlings to fully grown adults—have been recovered from the Gobi dunes.","Often credited historically as the likely real-world fossil inspiration behind the ancient mythological griffin described by Scythian gold miners and Greek travelers."]
sizeNotes: Based on abundant complete skeletons (e.g., AMNH 6251); adults reached ~1.8 to 2.0 meters.
sources: [{"citation":"Granger, W., & Gregory, W. K. (1923). Protoceratops andrewsi, a pre-ceratopsian dinosaur from Mongolia. American Museum Novitates, 72, 1-9.","url":"http://hdl.handle.net/2246/3233"},{"citation":"Fastovsky, D. E., Weishampel, D. B., Watabe, M., et al. (2011). A nest of juveniles of the basal ceratopsian dinosaur Protoceratops andrewsi from the Djadochta Formation (Late Cretaceous, Campanian), Tugrikinshireh, Mongolia. Journal of Paleontology, 85(6), 1035-1041.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1666/11-008.1"}]

name: Minmi
dietDetails: Herbivore specialized in low-level browsing, consuming seeds, fruiting bodies, small ferns, and fibrous vascular plants.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 1964 by Alan Bartholomai near Minmi Crossing, Roma, Queensland. Formally described by Ralph E. Molnar in 1980 (QM F10321) as Australia's first discovered armored dinosaur.
interestingFacts: ["Possesses unique horizontal bony rods running parallel along both sides of its backbone, termed \"paravertebrae\", which stiffened its spine while allowing rapid running.","Unlike the massive ankylosaurs of North America and Asia, Minmi was a small, agile Gondwanan quadruped measuring only 2.5 to 3.0 meters (8.2 to 10 feet) long.","Fossilized cololite (gut contents) preserved in an Australian specimen provided the direct microscopic evidence of dinosaur diet, showing cuticles of flowering plants, seeds, and fern spores.","Has the shortest generic dinosaur name alongside modern designations like Yi and Mei, honoring the indigenous Australian geographical locality of Minmi Crossing."]
sizeNotes: Based on holotype QM F10321; adult length ~2.5–3.0 meters.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/bad3e7d0-b8ce-4a7c-ada5-5c2f607ff661.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/bad3e7d0-b8ce-4a7c-ada5-5c2f607ff661","license":"Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0)","credit":"Cy Marchant","taxon":"Stegouros elengassen (Parankylosauria approximation)","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Molnar, R. E. (1980). An ankylosaur (Reptilia: Ornithischia) from the Lower Cretaceous of southern Queensland. Memoirs of the Queensland Museum, 20(1), 65-75.","url":"https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/part/303975"},{"citation":"Molnar, R. E., & Clifford, H. T. (2001). An ankylosaurian cololite from Queensland, Australia. In The Armored Dinosaurs (pp. 399-412). Indiana University Press.","url":"https://iupress.org/9780253339645/the-armored-dinosaurs/"}]

name: Elasmotherium
dietDetails: Hypsodont herbivorous grazer consuming abrasive dry steppe grasses, tubers, and herbs in sub-Arctic steppe environments.
geographicRange: {"continent":"Eurasia","region":"Pontic-Caspian Steppe & Siberia","country":"Russia, Kazakhstan, Ukraine","fossilFormation":"Late Pleistocene River Alluvium"}
discoveryHistory: First described in 1808 by Johann Fischer von Waldheim from a lower jaw in the Museum of Moscow University. Landmark ancient DNA research in 2018 established that it persisted until ~39,000 years ago.
interestingFacts: ["Popularly dubbed the \"Siberian Unicorn\", this enormous Pleistocene rhinoceros reached up to 5 meters in length and weighed between 3.5 and 5 metric tonnes.","Anchored a massive central cranial dome on its forehead that supported a gigantic keratinous horn, far larger than that of any living rhinoceros species.","High-resolution radiocarbon dating and ancient mitochondrial genome sequencing published in Nature (2018) proved it survived until approximately 39,000 years ago, directly coexisting with early modern humans and Neanderthals.","Possessed remarkably high-crowned (hypsodont) prismatic cheek teeth with complex enamel folding adapted specifically for grinding down silica-rich abrasive grasses."]
sizeNotes: Based on complete mounted skeletons in Russian paleontological institutions; shoulder height ~2.0–2.5 m.
sources: [{"citation":"Kosintsev, P., Mitchell, K. J., Devièse, T., et al. (2019). Evolution and extinction of the giant rhinoceros Elasmotherium sibiricum sheds light on late Quaternary megafaunal extinctions. Nature Ecology & Evolution, 3(1), 31-38.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1038/s41559-018-0722-0"}]

name: Nanaimoteuthis
dietDetails: Active pelagic predator and opportunistic detritivore feeding on crustaceans, small fish, and organic particles in deep marine shelf waters.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Cretaceous marine strata of the Haslam Formation on Vancouver Island, British Columbia. Described based on exceptionally preserved chitinous lower beaks by Dirk Fuchs, James W. Haggart, and René Hoffmann.
interestingFacts: ["An ancient Mesozoic relative of the enigmatic modern vampire squid (Vampyroteuthis infernalis), inhabiting the Pacific shelf seas during the Late Cretaceous.","Identified from remarkably preserved calcified lower jaws (beaks) exhibiting specialized hadrocheliate anatomy adapted for biting through crustacean carapaces.","Its generic name honors the Nanaimo Group geological sequence of British Columbia, while the species honors Geological Survey of Canada paleontologist James W. Haggart.","Demonstrates that coleoid cephalopods with vampire squid affinities occupied varied ecological niches across the Pacific rim tens of millions of years before modern deep-sea specialists."]
sizeNotes: Estimated from fossilized chitinous beak measurements; mantle length ~25–40 cm, total length ~0.8 m.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/a6be7f5c-82bb-42b8-8b17-fb0b8b2d277d.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/a6be7f5c-82bb-42b8-8b17-fb0b8b2d277d","license":"CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication","credit":"Kurtis Wothe and Giovanna Sainz","taxon":"Vampyroteuthis infernalis (Vampyromorpha approximation)","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}
sources: [{"citation":"Fuchs, D., Haggart, J. W., & Hoffmann, R. (2019). Nanaimoteuthis haggarti, a new vampyromorph coleoid from the Upper Cretaceous Haslam Formation of British Columbia, Canada. Cretaceous Research, 93, 303-310.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cretres.2018.09.019"}]

name: Lokiceratops
dietDetails: Herbivorous browser equipped with robust ceratopsid shearing dental batteries designed for slicing through fibrous cycads, palms, and woody angiosperms.
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Kennedy Coulee, Northern Montana","country":"United States","fossilFormation":"Judith River Formation"}
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 2019 in the Judith River Formation near the US-Canada border in northern Montana. Formally described in June 2024 by Mark A. Loewen, Joseph J.W. Sertich, and colleagues in the journal PeerJ.
interestingFacts: ["Described in 2024, Lokiceratops ranks among the largest centrosaurine ceratopsids ever discovered, stretching 6.7 meters (22 feet) long and weighing 5 tonnes with a skull over 2 meters in length.","Named after the Norse god Loki because of its massive, curving, blade-shaped frill horns that resemble Loki’s mythological bladed horned headgear.","Entirely lacked a nasal horn—a very unusual feature for centrosaurines—replacing it with the largest pair of curving epiparietal frill horns ever documented on a ceratopsian.","Coexisted simultaneously alongside four other distinct horned dinosaur species within the same river basin, demonstrating high regional endemism and ecological niche partitioning in Laramidia."]
sizeNotes: Based on holotype EMK 0012, an exceptionally preserved subadult/adult skull and postcrania.
sources: [{"citation":"Loewen, M. A., Sertich, J. J. W., Sampson, S., et al. (2024). Lokiceratops rangiformis gen. et sp. nov. (Ceratopsidae: Centrosaurinae) from the Campanian Judith River Formation of Montana reveals rapid turnover and high endemism in dinosaur communities. PeerJ, 12, e17224.","url":"https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.17224"}]

name: Dryptosaurus
dietDetails: Apex carnivorous predator preying on hadrosauroids (such as Hadrosaurus foulkii), nodosaurs, and small vertebrates of the Appalachian island continent.
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Appalachian Landmass","country":"United States (New Jersey)","fossilFormation":"Hornerstown / New Egypt Formation"}
discoveryHistory: Unearthed in 1866 by marl quarry workers in Mantua Township, New Jersey. Described by Edward Drinker Cope as "Laelaps", but renamed Dryptosaurus in 1877 by Othniel Charles Marsh because the name was preoccupied by a genus of mite.
interestingFacts: ["The apex predator of Appalachia—the isolated eastern North American landmass separated from Laramidia by the Western Interior Seaway during the Late Cretaceous.","Possessed enormous, laterally compressed 8-inch curved raptorial hand claws resembling eagle talons (giving rise to its species name aquilunguis), unlike the stunted arms of Tyrannosaurus rex.","Immortalized in 1897 by paleoartist Charles R. Knight in his legendary watercolor painting \"Leaping Laelaps\", which was the first artistic depiction to show dinosaurs as dynamic, athletic, warm-blooded animals.","Phylogenetic analyses demonstrate Dryptosaurus is a primitive tyrannosauroid that evolved independently in geographical isolation on Appalachia until the terminal K-Pg extinction event."]
sizeNotes: Based on holotype ANSP 9995; estimated adult length ~7.5 meters (25 feet).
sources: [{"citation":"Cope, E. D. (1866). On the remains of a gigantic extinct dinosaur, from the Cretaceous Green Sand of New Jersey. Proceedings of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia, 18, 275-279.","url":"https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/26298547"},{"citation":"Brusatte, S. L., Benson, R. B., & Norell, M. A. (2011). The anatomy and systematics of Dryptosaurus aquilunguis (Dinosauria: Theropoda)—a tyrannosauroid from the Cretaceous of North America. American Museum Novitates, 3717, 1-65.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1206/3717.2"}]

name: Dinocrocuta
dietDetails: Apex hypercarnivore and bone-crusher. Possessed immense pachyostotic premolars and jaw musculature capable of pulverizing thick limb bones of large rhinoceroses, proboscideans, and hipparion horses.
geographicRange: {"region":"Eurasia and North Africa","countries":["China","Greece","Turkey","Iran","Kazakhstan"],"fossilFormation":"Bahe Formation, Hezheng Basin, Pikermi Formation","coordinates":[35.5,103.2]}
discoveryHistory: First described by German paleontologist Max Schlosser in 1903 based on craniodental remains from northern China. Initially regarded as an enormous hyaenid, subsequent morphological and phylogenetic analyses demonstrated that Dinocrocuta represents a specialized branch of feliform carnivorans placed in the distinct family Percrocutidae.
interestingFacts: ["Dinocrocuta was one of the largest feliform bone-crushers to ever walk the Earth, weighing up to 380 kg (over four times the size of a modern spotted hyena).","Fossil evidence from the Linxia Basin revealed a female skull of the horned rhino Chilotherium bearing healed bite marks that perfectly match the conical premolars of Dinocrocuta, proving it actively hunted large megaherbivores rather than merely scavenging.","Its skull possessed massive sagittal crests and thickened zygomatic arches providing anchoring sites for bite forces exceeding that of modern lions and tigers."]
sizeNotes: Massive feliform carnivoran standing roughly 1.1–1.2 m at the shoulder, with an overall body length around 2.1 m and body mass estimates ranging from 300 to 400 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Schlosser, M. (1903). Die fossilen Säugethiere Chinas nebst einer Odontographie der recenten Antilopen. Abhandlungen der Bayerischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 22: 1-221.","url":"https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/89758"},{"citation":"Deng, T., & Tseng, Z. J. (2010). Osteological evidence for predatory behavior of the giant percrocutid Dinocrocuta gigantea as an active predator of rhinos. Chinese Science Bulletin, 55(17), 1790-1794.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1007/s11434-010-3031-9"}]

name: Hyaenodon
dietDetails: Specialized hypercarnivore with shear-like carnassial teeth adapted for cutting flesh and cracking bones of oreodonts, horses (Mesohippus), and early camels.
geographicRange: {"region":"North America","countries":["United States","Canada"],"fossilFormation":"White River Formation (Chadron & Brule Members), South Dakota and Nebraska","coordinates":[43.5,-102.5]}
discoveryHistory: Described by pioneering American paleontologist Joseph Leidy in 1853 from fossils collected in the White River Badlands of South Dakota. Despite its name, Hyaenodon is not related to modern hyenas, belonging instead to the extinct placental order Hyaenodonta.
interestingFacts: ["Hyaenodon horridus had an extraordinarily elongated skull with powerful jaw muscles that produced a shearing scissor action with its fourth upper premolar and first lower molar.","Unlike true carnivorans which shed milk teeth and retain a single pair of carnassials, Hyaenodon replaced its shearing teeth in sequential waves, allowing it to maintain sharp cutting edges throughout its lifespan.","Endocranial cast studies reveal that Hyaenodon had a well-developed olfactory bulb and acute sense of smell, though its cerebrum was proportionally smaller than that of modern carnivorans."]
sizeNotes: Substantial mammalian predator measuring approximately 1.7 m in total length, 0.75 m at the shoulder, and weighing around 60 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Leidy, J. (1853). The ancient fauna of Nebraska: or, a description of results of extensive collections of extinct mammalia and chelonia. Smithsonian Contributions to Knowledge, 6: 1-126.","url":"https://doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.12461"},{"citation":"Mellett, J. S. (1977). Paleobiology of North American Hyaenodon (Mammalia, Creodonta). Contributions to Vertebrate Evolution, 1: 1-134.","url":"https://link.springer.com/book/9783805523790"}]

name: Inostrancevia africana
nameMeaning: Inostrantsev's beast from Africa (honoring Alexander Inostrantsev + geographic origin)
dietDetails: Apex saber-toothed therapsid. Preyed upon large herbivorous pareiasaurs (such as Pareiasuchus) and dicynodonts using massive, laterally compressed canine tusks designed to inflict devastating slashing puncture wounds.
geographicRange: {"region":"Southern Gondwana","countries":["South Africa"],"fossilFormation":"Balfour Formation (Daptocephalus Assemblage Zone), Karoo Basin","coordinates":[-31.5,25.5]}
discoveryHistory: Described in 2023 by Christian Kammerer and colleagues from two specimens discovered in South Africa’s Karoo Basin. This remarkable find proved that Russian apex gorgonopsians migrated over 11,000 kilometers across supercontinent Pangaea to southern Gondwana shortly before the end-Permian mass extinction.
interestingFacts: ["Inostrancevia africana represents an extraordinary example of rapid intercontinental migration across Pangaea during the ecological destabilization leading up to the Great Dying.","Prior to its 2023 discovery in South Africa, Inostrancevia was thought to be strictly restricted to the Late Permian deposits of European Russia (Sokolki faunal complex).","The invasion of Inostrancevia into southern Africa temporarily replaced local African rubidgeine gorgonopsians as the undisputed apex predator of the Karoo Basin just before all gorgonopsians were wiped out."]
sizeNotes: Large gorgonopsian reaching roughly 3.0 m in length, 1.1 m in height, with an estimated body mass around 300 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Kammerer, C. F., Viglietti, P. A., Butler, E. D., & Botha, J. (2023). Rapid turnover of top predators in African terrestrial faunas around the Permian-Triassic boundary. Current Biology, 33(11), 2283-2290.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2023.04.050"}]

name: Lystrosaurus georgi
nameMeaning: Shovel lizard of Georgi (Greek lystron "shovel" + sauros "lizard")
dietDetails: Low-browsing, digging herbivore with a horny beak and twin maxillary tusks used for slicing tough roots, tubers, ferns, and equisetaleans.
geographicRange: {"region":"European Russia","countries":["Russia"],"fossilFormation":"Vetlugian Superhorizon, Vologda and Nizhny Novgorod Oblasts","coordinates":[58.5,45]}
discoveryHistory: Described by Russian paleontologist Nikolai Kalandadze in 1975 from cranial and postcranial material recovered in the Vetluga river basin of European Russia. It proved that Lystrosaurus was a truly cosmopolitan survivor of the Permian-Triassic extinction across northern Laurasia as well as southern Gondwana.
interestingFacts: ["Lystrosaurus is famous as the quintessential \"disaster taxon,\" surviving the Permian-Triassic extinction when 95% of species died, and proliferating to make up to 90% of all land vertebrates in some Early Triassic ecosystems.","Lystrosaurus georgi possessed a distinctive, strongly downturned snout and reinforced cranial sutures adapted for heavy grubbing and subterranean foraging.","Histological bone studies indicate Lystrosaurus grew rapidly and was capable of metabolic torpor or hibernation in burrows, which likely enabled it to endure catastrophic post-impact climate swings."]
sizeNotes: Robust, barrel-bodied herbivorous synapsid measuring approximately 2.0 m in length, 0.8 m in shoulder height, and weighing up to 150 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Kalandadze, N. N. (1975). The first discovery of Lystrosaurus in the European regions of the USSR. Paleontological Journal, 4: 140-142.","url":"https://eurekamag.com/research/005/737/005737152.php"},{"citation":"Botha-Brink, J. (2017). Burrowing in Lystrosaurus: preadaptation to a post-extinction world? Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology, 37(6): e1380414.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1080/02724634.2017.1380414"}]

name: Amphicyon
dietDetails: Apex bone-crushing omnivore/hypercarnivore. Possessed massive canine and molars capable of subduing large ungulates (chalicotheres, proto-horses, camels) and crushing large marrow-bearing bones.
geographicRange: {"region":"North America","countries":["United States"],"fossilFormation":"Sheep Creek Formation, Olcott Formation, Nebraska and California","coordinates":[41.5,-103.5]}
discoveryHistory: Amphicyon ingens was described by William Diller Matthew in 1924 based on exceptional Miocene remains from Sioux County, Nebraska. Colloquially termed "bear-dogs," amphicyonids combined the heavily muscled forequarters and plantigrade/semi-plantigrade hindquarters of bears with the skull and dentition of canids.
interestingFacts: ["Amphicyon ingens was the largest known bear-dog in North America, reaching estimated body masses of up to 450–600 kg, rivaling the largest modern brown bears.","Unlike true dogs, Amphicyon had heavy, robust limb bones and plantigrade feet, meaning it was an ambush predator rather than a pursuit runner.","Its forelimbs had high rotational flexibility, allowing it to wrestle large struggling megaherbivores to the ground before applying crushing fatal bites."]
sizeNotes: Massive, muscular predator measuring 2.5 m in head-body length, 1.2 m at the shoulder, and weighing approximately 450–550 kg.
extinctionEvent: Late Miocene grassland expansion and faunal turnover
sources: [{"citation":"Matthew, W. D. (1924). Third contribution to the Snake Creek fauna. name: Thylacosmilus
nameMeaning: Pouched knife (Greek thylakos "pouch" + smile "carving knife") - atrox "terrible/fierce"
dietDetails: Hyper-specialized soft-tissue predator. Possessed ever-growing dagger-like canines with immense mandibular protective flanges, using its muscular neck to drive sabers into soft visceral organs of notoungulates.
discoveryHistory: Named by Elmer S. Riggs in 1933 from fossils collected during the Field Museum Marshall Field Paleontological Expeditions to Catamarca Province, Argentina. It is the most famous example of convergent evolution toward a saber-toothed morphology among non-placental metatherians.
interestingFacts: ["Unlike placental saber-toothed cats (like Smilodon), Thylacosmilus had continuously growing, rootless canines whose roots arched back over the eye orbits into the skull roof.","Its lower jaw featured enormous downward-projecting flanges of bone (symphysial flanges) that protected the elongated canines when the mouth was closed.","Biomechanically, Thylacosmilus had relatively weak jaw closing muscles but immensely powerful neck depressor musculature, indicating it used its entire neck and head like a sledgehammer to drive its canines into prey."]
sizeNotes: Jaguar-sized metatherian carnivore measuring approximately 1.5 m in length, 0.65 m at the shoulder, and weighing 80–120 kg.
extinctionEvent: Great American Biotic Interchange (GABI) faunal turnover
sources: [{"citation":"Riggs, E. S. (1934). A new marsupial saber-tooth from the Pliocene of Argentina and its relationships to other South American sparassodonts. name: Masiakasaurus
nameMeaning: Vicious lizard of Knopfler (Malagasy masiaka "vicious" + Mark Knopfler)
dietDetails: Piscivore and small-vertebrate specialist. Unique forward-projecting (procumbent) anterior teeth were designed for snagging slippery fish, frogs, lizards, and small mammals.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by a joint expedition from Stony Brook University and the University of Antananarivo and described by Scott Sampson, Matthew Carrano, and Catherine Forster in 2001. The species epithet honors musician Mark Knopfler, whose Dire Straits music the expedition crew was playing when the holotype was discovered.
interestingFacts: ["Masiakasaurus possessed one of the most bizarre dental specializations among all theropods: its front teeth projected almost horizontally forward out of its lower jaw.","Its anterior teeth were spoon-shaped with hook-like tips, functioning as an effective grasping trap for gripping fast, slippery prey like freshwater fish and crustaceans.","Unlike long-legged cursorial coelurosaurs, Masiakasaurus had relatively short, robust limbs and may have had an amphibious or low-slung hunting posture along riverbanks."]
sizeNotes: Small, slender noasaurid theropod reaching roughly 1.8–2.0 m in length, 0.65 m in hip height, and weighing around 35–45 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Sampson, S. D., Carrano, M. T., & Forster, C. A. (2001). A bizarre predatory dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Madagascar. name: Megacerops
nameMeaning: Large-horned face (Greek megas "large" + keras "horn" + ops "face") of Colorado
dietDetails: Browser of soft vegetation, forest leaves, young twigs, and succulent fruits, aided by low-crowned (brachydont) teeth.
geographicRange: {"region":"North America","countries":["United States","Canada"],"fossilFormation":"Chadron Formation, White River Badlands, South Dakota and Colorado","coordinates":[40.5,-104.5]}
discoveryHistory: Originally named by Joseph Leidy in 1870 from fossils found in Colorado. Over subsequent decades, dozens of specimens were described under various synonyms including Brontotherium, Titanotherium, and Menodus before taxonomic revisions established Megacerops as the valid senior genus.
interestingFacts: ["Megacerops sported a distinctive Y-shaped nasal horn made of solid bone, which was significantly larger and blunt in adult males and smaller in females.","Cracked and healed rib fossils on adult male Megacerops specimens demonstrate that they used their blunt nasal horns to shove and butt each other during intraspecific mating battles.","Despite strongly resembling modern rhinoceroses, Megacerops belonged to the extinct family Brontotheriidae and was more closely related to horses than rhinos."]
sizeNotes: Colossal perissodactyl mammal standing 2.5 m tall at the shoulder, reaching 5.0 m in length, and weighing up to 3,300 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Leidy, J. (1870). Remarks on a collection of fossils from the western territories. name: Cervalces
dietDetails: Herbivore specialized in aquatic vegetation, wetland sedges, willow, birch, and swamp flora in periglacial spruce parks and boreal wetlands.
geographicRange: {"region":"North America","countries":["United States","Canada"],"fossilFormation":"Post-glacial lacustrine and bog sediments (e.g., New Jersey, Ohio, Iowa, Ontario)","coordinates":[40.8,-74.4]}
discoveryHistory: First discovered in 1885 by William Berryman Scott at Mount Hermon, New Jersey, from an extraordinarily complete post-glacial skeleton. Scott originally identified it as a distinct genus combining anatomical characteristics of both elk (wapiti) and moose, hence the common name "stag-moose".
interestingFacts: ["Cervalces scotti had the most intricate antlers of any known deer: each antler branched into three distinct palmated lobes with complex curved tines, spanning up to 2.5 meters across.","It was noticeably taller and longer-legged than modern moose, standing around 2.0 m at the shoulder with a head profile resembling that of an elk.","Cervalces coexisted with early Paleo-Indian hunters in North America before vanishing around 11,500 years ago during the Quaternary extinction event."]
sizeNotes: Large deer standing roughly 2.0 m at the shoulder, 2.5 m in total length, and weighing around 700 kg.

name: Synthetoceras
nameMeaning: Combined horn (Greek synthetos "combined" + keras "horn") with three horns
dietDetails: Herbivorous browser and grazer feeding on shrubs, grasses, and forbs across open woodland savannahs.
geographicRange: {"region":"North America","countries":["United States"],"fossilFormation":"Clarendon Formation, Ogallala Group, Texas and Nebraska","coordinates":[34.9,-100.9]}
discoveryHistory: Described by paleontologist R. A. Stirton in 1932 from spectacular Miocene cranial material recovered in the Texas panhandle. Synthetoceras is the largest and most derived member of the extinct artiodactyl family Protoceratidae.
interestingFacts: ["Synthetoceras possessed one of the most unusual horn arrangements of any mammal: a long, forward-pointing rostral horn on its snout that split at its tip into a dramatic, forked Y-shape.","In addition to its bizarre nasal fork, Synthetoceras had two curved, backward-sweeping horns behind its eyes above the brow.","Only adult males possessed the giant forked rostral horn, indicating it was primarily a display structure and weapon for rival shoving matches during the mating season."]
sizeNotes: Antelope-like artiodactyl measuring roughly 2.0 m in length, 1.1 m at the shoulder, and weighing around 180–220 kg.

name: Dinofelis
nameMeaning: Terrible cat (Greek deinos "terrible" + Latin felis "cat") of Barlow
dietDetails: Apex ambush predator with robust forelimbs and flattened, semi-saber canines. Preyed upon medium to large ungulates, primates, and early hominins (Australopithecus and Paranthropus).
geographicRange: {"region":"Southern and Eastern Africa","countries":["South Africa","Kenya","Ethiopia","Tanzania"],"fossilFormation":"Sterkfontein, Swartkrans, and Kromdraai cave deposits (Cradle of Humankind)","coordinates":[-26,27.7]}
discoveryHistory: Named by famed Scottish paleontologist Robert Broom in 1937 from fossils discovered at the Sterkfontein cave system in South Africa. Dinofelis is a member of the tribe Metailurini, representing "false saber-toothed cats" with intermediate canine lengths.
interestingFacts: ["Fossil baboon and early hominin skull fragments from South African caves exhibit puncture marks matching the canine spacing of Dinofelis, earning it the reputation of an active predator of our early ancestors.","Unlike cursorial cats like cheetahs, Dinofelis possessed heavily built forelimbs and a stocky body build reminiscent of a jaguar, perfectly suited for ambush hunting in mixed woodland environments.","Its canines were flattened and serrated but shorter than those of Smilodon, making them less prone to accidental breakage when grappling live prey."]
sizeNotes: Jaguar-sized machairodontine cat measuring 1.8 m in body length, 0.85 m at the shoulder, and weighing around 110–130 kg.

name: Geosternbergia
dietDetails: Aerial ocean-forager feeding on marine fish, squid, and belemnites dip-netted from the surface waters of the Western Interior Seaway.
geographicRange: {"region":"North America","countries":["United States"],"fossilFormation":"Niobrara Formation (Smoky Hill Chalk Member), Kansas","coordinates":[38.8,-99.5]}
discoveryHistory: Originally discovered in 1952 by famous fossil hunter George F. Sternberg in Graham County, Kansas, and classified by Harksen as Pteranodon sternbergi. In 2010, Alexander Kellner erected the distinct genus Geosternbergia to recognize its upright cranial crest and morphological divergence from Pteranodon longiceps.
interestingFacts: ["Geosternbergia males possessed an immense, upright cranial crest that stood vertically above the skull like a sail, reaching heights of over 1 meter.","Females possessed much smaller, rounded crests and wider pelvic canals for laying eggs, providing one of the clearest examples of sexual dimorphism among pterosaurs.","Despite having a colossal wingspan of 6 meters (20 feet), its pneumatic hollow bones and ultralight skeleton meant it weighed only 20–30 kg."]
sizeNotes: Spectacular pteranodontid pterosaur with a wingspan of 6.0 m, standing 1.8 m tall on the ground, and weighing around 25 kg.
comparisonSilhouette: {"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-silhouettes/071babce-127c-4e5d-8472-62e17ad1e7e1.svg","sourceUrl":"https://www.phylopic.org/images/071babce-127c-4e5d-8472-62e17ad1e7e1","license":"Attribution 4.0 International","credit":"Matthew Dempsey","taxon":"Pteranodontidae (Representative: Pteranodon)","taxonMatch":"generic approximation, not species-specific"}

name: Megaloceros
dietDetails: Mixed feeder and grazer consuming nutrient-rich grasses, willow, birch, forbs, and water plants rich in calcium and phosphorus needed for antler mineralization.
geographicRange: {"region":"Eurasia and North Africa","countries":["Ireland","United Kingdom","Germany","Russia","China"],"fossilFormation":"Ballybetagh Bog (Ireland), periglacial loess and lacustrine deposits across Eurasia","coordinates":[53.2,-6.2]}
discoveryHistory: Colloquially known as the "Irish Elk", Megaloceros was first scientifically named Cervus giganteus by Johann Friedrich Blumenbach in 1799 based on numerous intact skeletons preserved in Irish peat bogs. Georges Cuvier famously studied its skeleton to establish that extinction was a real biological phenomenon.
interestingFacts: ["Megaloceros grew the largest antlers of any known deer: male antlers spanned up to 3.65 meters (12 feet) from tip to tip and weighed over 40 kilograms (88 pounds).","Males had to regenerate this colossal bony headgear from scratch every single year, requiring immense nutritional intake of calcium and phosphate during the summer growing season.","Ancient Paleolithic humans depicted Megaloceros in vivid cave paintings (such as at Chauvet and Lascaux), revealing a distinctive dark dorsal hump and neck coloration."]
sizeNotes: Enormous cervid standing 2.1 m tall at the shoulder, with total length of 3.1 m and weight up to 700 kg, carrying antlers spanning up to 3.65 m.
extinctionEvent: Holocene extinction of Eurasian megafauna (survived in Urals until ~7,700 years ago)
sources: [{"citation":"Lister, A. M. (1994). The evolution of the giant deer, Megaloceros giganteus (Blumenbach). Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society, 112(1-2), 65-100.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1096-3642.1994.tb00312.x"},{"citation":"Stuart, A. J., et al. (2004). Pleistocene to Holocene extinction dynamics in giant deer and woolly mammoth. Nature, 431(7009), 684-689.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1038/nature02890"}]

name: Kaprosuchus
nameMeaning: Boar crocodile of the Sahara (Greek kapros "boar" + souchos "crocodile")
dietDetails: Terrestrial cursorial predator. Preyed upon ornithopods, juvenile sauropods, and terrestrial vertebrates using hypertrophied, caniniform tusk-like teeth that meshed outside the jaws.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 2000 during a National Geographic expedition led by Paul Sereno in the Sahara Desert of Niger, and formally described in 2009. Sereno coined the popular nickname "BoarCroc" due to its extraordinary sets of dagger-like boar-like tusks.
interestingFacts: ["Kaprosuchus earned its nickname \"BoarCroc\" from three pairs of enlarged caniniform teeth, including huge lower tusks that slotted into deep notches in the upper rostrum.","Unlike modern semi-aquatic crocodilians, Kaprosuchus had forward-facing stereoscopic eyes positioned on the sides rather than the top of the skull, indicating it was an active terrestrial pursuit hunter.","Its heavily armored skull had reinforced fused nasal bones that allowed it to deliver bone-shattering ramming bites without dislocating its jaws."]
sizeNotes: Active terrestrial crocodylomorph measuring roughly 3.3 m in length, 0.9 m in height, and weighing around 250 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Sereno, P. C., & Larsson, H. C. (2009). Cretaceous crocodyliforms from the Sahara. ZooKeys, 28: 1-143.","url":"https://doi.org/10.3897/zookeys.28.325"}]

name: Sarcosuchus
nameMeaning: Flesh crocodile emperor (Greek sarx "flesh" + souchos "crocodile" + Latin imperator "emperor")
dietDetails: Apex riverine ambush predator and piscivore. Consumed gigantic freshwater fish (Mawsonia, Lepidotes) and ambushed medium-to-large dinosaurs (Ouranosaurus, nigersaurids) drinking at riverbanks.
discoveryHistory: First discovered by French paleontologist Albert-Félix de Lapparent in the Sahara and named in 1966 by France de Broin and Philippe Taquet. In 1997 and 2000, Paul Sereno recovered extraordinary complete skulls and skeletons from Niger, giving the world a comprehensive anatomical understanding of "SuperCroc".
interestingFacts: ["Sarcosuchus imperator is colloquially known as \"SuperCroc\"—its skull alone measured up to 1.6 meters (5.2 feet) long, lined with 132 stout, conical teeth.","The tip of its snout terminated in an expanded bulbous enclosure called the bulla, which may have housed an olfactory resonating chamber for underwater territorial communication.","Growth ring analysis of its osteoderms indicates that Sarcosuchus grew continuously for over 40 to 50 years to achieve its massive adult size of 9.5 meters."]
sizeNotes: One of the largest crocodylomorphs that ever lived, measuring 9.5 m in length, 1.3 m in standing height, and weighing approximately 3,500 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Sereno, P. C., et al. (2001). The giant crocodyliform Sarcosuchus from the Cretaceous of Africa. Science, 294(5546), 1516-1519.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1066521"},{"citation":"O'Brien, H. D., et al. (2019). Crocodylian head gear: ontogeny, sexual dimorphism, and biomechanical implications of cranial ornamentation in Sarcosuchus. The Anatomical Record, 303(4): 989-1002.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1002/ar.24151"}]

name: Barinasuchus
nameMeaning: Barinas crocodile (State of Barinas, Venezuela + Alberto Arvelo Torrealba)
dietDetails: Apex terrestrial hypercarnivore. Possessed ziphodont (blade-like, laterally compressed, recurved, serrated) teeth designed to carve devastating slashing wounds through large South American notoungulates, astrapotheres, and litopterns.
geographicRange: {"region":"South America","countries":["Venezuela","Peru","Argentina"],"fossilFormation":"Parángula Formation (Venezuela), Ipururo Formation (Peru), Divisadero Largo Formation (Argentina)","coordinates":[8.6,-70.2]}
discoveryHistory: Described in 2007 by Alfredo Paolillo and Omar Linares based on a massive, deep-snouted partial skull from the Parángula Formation in Barinas State, Venezuela. Additional finds in Peru and Argentina confirmed Barinasuchus as the largest known sebecid and the largest terrestrial predator in Cenozoic South America.
interestingFacts: ["Barinasuchus is the largest terrestrial carnivore known from the entire Cenozoic Era, surpassing in size even the giant terror birds (Phorusrhacidae) and sparassodonts.","Unlike modern semi-aquatic crocodiles with broad, flattened skulls, Barinasuchus had an extraordinarily tall, laterally compressed skull (oreinirostral) with an erect, pillar-erect quadrupedal stance.","Its ziphodont teeth were serrated like steak knives, virtually indistinguishable in functional morphology from the teeth of carcharodontosaurid theropod dinosaurs."]
sizeNotes: Colossal terrestrial sebecid crocodylomorph reaching 6.3 m in total length, 1.4 m at the hip, with an estimated body mass of 1,700 kg.

name: Entelodon
timePeriod: Early to Late Oligocene (Rupelian to Chattian)
dietDetails: Apex opportunistic omnivore and bone-crushing scavenger. Devoured tough roots, carcasses, tubers, nuts, and small to medium mammals, using heavily worn crushing molars.
discoveryHistory: Named by French naturalist Auguste Aymard in 1846 from fossil deposits in Ronzon near Le Puy-en-Velay, France. Entelodon gave its name to the family Entelodontidae, popularly called "hell pigs" or "terminator pigs," although phylogenetic studies place them closer to hippopotamuses and cetaceans than true pigs.
interestingFacts: ["Entelodon had massive bony cheek flanges (jugal bosses) projecting outward from its skull, which anchored crushing jaw muscles and protected its eyes during violent territorial combats.","Fossil skulls of Entelodon frequently exhibit deep bite wounds and scarred bone punctures inflicted by the canines of other entelodonts, indicating aggressive face-biting behavior.","Despite their popular nickname \"hell pigs,\" genetic and morphological analyses reveal that entelodonts were more closely related to hippos and whales (Cetancodonta) than to true swine (Suidae)."]
sizeNotes: Formidable, hump-shouldered entelodont measuring roughly 2.7 m in length, 1.35 m at the shoulder, and weighing around 450 kg.

name: Sarkastodon
nameMeaning: Flesh-tearing tooth (Greek sarx "flesh" + kazo "to tear/rend" + odon "tooth") of Mongolia
dietDetails: Apex hypercarnivorous bone-crusher and ambush predator. Specialized in tackling large Eocene megaherbivores such as brontotheres, chalicotheres, and early rhinocerotoids.
geographicRange: {"region":"Central and East Asia","countries":["Mongolia","China"],"fossilFormation":"Irdin Manha Formation, Inner Mongolia, and Ergilin Dzo Formation, Mongolia","coordinates":[43.6,111.9]}
discoveryHistory: Discovered during the Central Asiatic Expeditions of the American Museum of Natural History led by Roy Chapman Andrews in the Gobi Desert, and described by Walter Granger in 1938. Sarkastodon is the largest known member of the extinct order Oxyaenida.
interestingFacts: ["Sarkastodon was one of the largest mammalian carnivores of the Eocene, with skull lengths of up to 53 centimeters (21 inches) and estimated body masses of 600–800 kg.","Unlike carnivorans whose shearing teeth are the 4th upper premolar and 1st lower molar, oxyaenids like Sarkastodon developed carnassials further back on their first upper and second lower molars.","Its teeth were stout and blunt with heavy enamel wrinkling, functioning like crushing shears to pulverize bones and heavy hide."]
sizeNotes: Massive, bear-like oxyaenid measuring approximately 3.0 m in length, 1.3 m at the shoulder, and weighing 700–800 kg.

name: Deinotherium
dietDetails: High-browsing folivore. Used downward-curving mandibular tusks and a muscular trunk to strip bark, branches, and high forest canopy foliage.
discoveryHistory: Named by Johann Jakob Kaup in 1829 from teeth and skulls discovered near Eppelsheim, Germany. Kaup was baffled by the downward-hooking lower jaw tusks and initially mounted them pointing upward or backward before articulated skeletons confirmed their downturned orientation.
interestingFacts: ["Deinotherium had no upper tusks at all; instead, it grew two massive tusks from its lower jaw that curved sharply downward and backward.","These downward-facing tusks functioned as natural pruning hooks, allowing Deinotherium to hook high tree branches and strip tough bark from tree trunks.","Standing over 4 meters (13 feet) at the shoulder and weighing up to 12 metric tons, Deinotherium giganteum was one of the largest terrestrial mammals ever to exist."]
sizeNotes: Towering proboscidean standing roughly 4.0 m at the shoulder, with total length of 6.5 m and weight reaching 10,000–12,000 kg.
extinctionEvent: Pleistocene cooling and forest habitat reduction

name: Jaekelopterus
nameMeaning: Otto Jaekel's wing of the Rhineland (German paleontologist Otto Jaekel + Greek pteron "wing")
dietDetails: Apex aquatic hypercarnivore and apex predator. Hunted early jawless and placoderm fish and smaller eurypterids using massive, toothed cheliceral claws with immense crushing speed.
geographicRange: {"region":"Western Europe and North America","countries":["Germany","United States"],"fossilFormation":"Klerf Formation (Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany), Beartooth Butte Formation (Wyoming)","coordinates":[50.2,6.5]}
discoveryHistory: First described by German paleontologist Otto Jaekel in 1914 from Devonian strata in the Rhineland, and subsequently placed in the genus Jaekelopterus by Charles D. Waterston in 1964. In 2007, Simon Braddy and colleagues announced the discovery of a giant 46-centimeter cheliceral claw from Willwerath, Germany, demonstrating that Jaekelopterus reached a staggering 2.5 meters in total body length, making it the largest arthropod ever discovered.
interestingFacts: ["Jaekelopterus rhenaniae was the largest arthropod known to have ever lived on Earth, reaching an astonishing length of 2.5 to 2.6 meters (8.2 to 8.5 feet).","Its immense pincers (chelicerae) alone measured 46 centimeters (18 inches) in length, equipped with sharp serrated denticles designed to cut and seize armored placoderm fish.","Unlike modern horseshoe crabs and scorpions, Jaekelopterus had large, specialized compound eyes capable of stereoscopic vision and high visual acuity for ambush hunting in brackish estuarine river deltas."]
sizeNotes: Colossal eurypterid arthropod reaching 2.5 m in total length, with a body width of 0.7 m and estimated body mass around 40 kg.
extinctionEvent: Late Devonian extinction events (Kellwasser / Hangenberg events)

name: Microraptor
nameMeaning: Tiny thief of Zhao (Greek mikros "small" + Latin raptor "thief" + Zhao Zichao)
dietDetails: Agile arboreal hunter and opportunistic predator. Fossilized stomach contents preserved within Microraptor specimens demonstrate a broad diet including enantiornithine birds, small mammals, fish, and arboreal lizards.
geographicRange: {"region":"East Asia","countries":["China"],"fossilFormation":"Jiufotang and Yixian Formations (Jehol Biota), Liaoning Province","coordinates":[41.5,120.5]}
discoveryHistory: First described in 2000 by Xu Xing, Zhou Zhonghe, and Wang Xiaolin from spectacular fossil slabs preserving delicate feather impressions in the Jiufotang Formation of Liaoning, China. In 2003, additional specimens revealed asymmetrical flight feathers on both forelimbs and hindlimbs, providing the first definitive evidence of a "four-winged" dinosaur capable of gliding and powered flight.
interestingFacts: ["Microraptor is famous as the \"four-winged dinosaur,\" bearing asymmetrical aerodynamic flight feathers on both its forelimbs and hindlimbs.","In 2012, scanning electron microscopy of fossilized melanosomes preserved in its plumage revealed that Microraptor had iridescent, glossy black feathers with a metallic sheen similar to modern crows.","Spectacular fossil stomach contents show that Microraptor hunted in trees and along lakeshores, with preserved digestive remains of perching birds, teleost fish, and early mammals."]
sizeNotes: Small four-winged dromaeosaurid measuring 0.8 m in total length (including tail plume), 0.3 m in standing height, and weighing roughly 1 kg.

name: Aquilops
dietDetails: Herbivorous browser consuming low-lying Cretaceous vegetation, ferns, cycads, and early flowering angiosperms.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1997 by Scott Madsen during a paleontological expedition in the Cloverly Formation of Carbon County, Montana.
• Formally described in 2014 by Andrew A. Farke, W. Desmond Maxwell, Richard L. Cifelli, and Mathew J. Wedel.
• Represents the oldest definitive neoceratopsian known from North America, predating later horned dinosaurs like Zuniceratops by ~15-20 million years.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in Montana's Cloverly Formation, Aquilops is the oldest definitive neoceratopsian dinosaur found in North America, dating to approximately 109–104 million years ago.","Measuring only ~60 cm (2 ft) in length and weighing an estimated 1.5 kg (3.3 lb), Aquilops was remarkably small—roughly the mass of a modern domestic rabbit or crow.","Its genus name translates to 'eagle face' (Latin aquila and Greek ops), referencing its strongly hooked rostral beak with a distinctive small bump or hornlet protruding forward from its snout.","Phylogenetically, Aquilops is more closely related to Asian basal neoceratopsians (such as Liaoceratops and Archaeoceratops) than to later North American ceratopsids, providing direct evidence of an early Cretaceous faunal migration event between Asia and North America."]
sizeNotes: One of the smallest known ceratopsians, about 60 cm in body length and 1.5 kg in weight.
sources: [{"citation":"Farke, A. A., Maxwell, W. D., Cifelli, R. L., & Wedel, M. J. (2014). A Ceratopsian Dinosaur from the Lower Cretaceous of Western North America, and the Biogeography of Neoceratopsia. PLoS ONE, 9(12), e112055.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0112055"},{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) - Aquilops americanus (Record #310860)","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=310860"}]

name: Dsungaripterus
dietDetails: Specialized durophage feeding on hard-shelled mollusks, crustaceans, and fish using toothless hooked beak tips to extract prey and flat bulbous rear teeth to crush shells.
discoveryHistory:
• First described in 1964 by pioneering Chinese paleontologist Yang Zhongjian (C.C. Young) based on a skull and partial skeleton from the Junggar Basin in Xinjiang, China.
• The species was named Dsungaripterus weii in honor of paleontologist C.M. Wei.
• In 1973, additional excavations in the Shengjinkou Formation recovered nearly complete skulls and articulated postcrania.
• Recognized as the type genus of the family Dsungaripteridae, known for their unique upward-curving beaks and crushing rear dentition.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed prominent upturned, toothless beak tips used to probe sediments and pry open hard-shelled mollusks and crustaceans from rocky lakeshores.","Unlike most fish-eating pterosaurs with needle-sharp teeth, Dsungaripterus had broad, bulbous, flat-crowned teeth at the rear of its jaws specialized for shell-crushing durophagy.","A distinctive low bony crest ran along the midline of its skull from the middle of the snout backward to a pointed occipital crest overhanging the neck.","Possessed exceptionally thick-walled limb bones and stout proportions, indicating that it was capable of proficient quadrupedal terrestrial locomotion on land."]
sizeNotes: Wingspan of approximately 3.0–3.5 m (9.8–11.5 ft), standing height around 1.2 m, and estimated body weight of 25–35 kg with robust, thick-walled flight bones.

name: Yuxisaurus
nameMeaning: Yuxi lizard (named after Yuxi, Yunnan, China; honoring biologist John J. Kopchick)
dietDetails: Herbivorous low-level browser feeding on ferns, cycads, and early seed plants using small leaf-shaped dentition.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Lower Jurassic Fengjiahe Formation of Yuxi, Yunnan Province, southwestern China.
• Formally described in 2022 by Xi Yao, Paul M. Barrett, Xing Xu, and colleagues based on holotype CVEB 21701 (partial skeleton with over 120 osteoderms).
• Represents the first confirmed, well-preserved early-diverging armored dinosaur (basal thyreophoran) discovered in the Early Jurassic of Asia.
interestingFacts: ["The first definitively identified early-diverging thyreophoran (armored dinosaur) from the Early Jurassic of Asia, dating to ~199–183 Ma.","Preserved with more than 120 bony dermal armor plates (osteoderms) of varying shapes, including keeled scutes, spine-like armor, and pup-tent-shaped plates along its back and neck.","Possessed heavily built forelimbs and robust pectoral girdle elements, demonstrating that early thyreophorans had already evolved specialized quadrupedal weight support.","Phylogenetic analyses place Yuxisaurus as a basal thyreophoran closely related to the European Emausaurus and Scelidosaurus, or alternatively as a basal parankylosaur sharing specialized cervical armor."]
sizeNotes: Estimated adult length of approximately 2.0–3.0 m (6.6–9.8 ft), standing ~0.8 m tall, with a heavily armored body covered in over 120 osteoderms.
